MIN_LENGTH comes from the auth service, or the // NIST SP 800-63B-4 default for password-only sign-in. isCommonPassword() checks a short // list on the client; the full breached-password check runs on the server. const MIN_LENGTH = 15;  function getPasswordRequirementState(password, isCommonPassword) {   const length = [...password].length; // count Unicode code points, not UTF-16 units   if (length === 0) return 'none';   if (length < MIN_LENGTH) return 'too-short';   if (isCommonPassword(password)) return 'too-common';   return 'meets-requirements'; }

Show password

  • A <button type="button"> next to the field, named "Show password", with aria-pressed. Its name stays the same, screen readers announce its state, and focus stays on it. A "Show password" checkbox works too.
  • Password fields have spellcheck="false" and autocapitalize="none". Shown as text, a password could otherwise reach a browser's online spell-check service (Chrome's Enhanced Spell Check and Microsoft Editor, when turned on; reported in 2022).
  • The password is hidden again when the form is sent or reset, and when the page comes back from the back/forward cache, so it's never left showing.
// The show-password button: a toggle with a name that stays the same and aria-pressed, so // screen readers announce its state, and focus stays on it. The password is hidden again // when the form is sent or reset, and when the page comes back from the back/forward cache. const password = document.getElementById('sign-in-password'); const toggle = document.querySelector('[aria-controls="sign-in-password"]');  function setShown(shown) {   password.type = shown ? 'text' : 'password';   toggle.setAttribute('aria-pressed', String(shown)); }  toggle.addEventListener('click', () => setShown(password.type === 'password')); password.form.addEventListener('submit', () => setShown(false)); password.form.addEventListener('reset', () => setShown(false)); // hiding is always safe window.addEventListener('pageshow', (event) => {   if (event.persisted) setShown(false); });

Messages that stay generic

These never reveal whether an email has an account, and read the same for every account:

  • Rejected sign-in: "Email or password is incorrect", without saying which field was wrong.
  • Network or service failure: "Unable to sign in right now. Try again shortly". It doesn't blame the password, so an outage never sends people to reset it.
  • After registration: "Check your email to continue", for new and existing emails alike; the backend emails the existing account's owner instead. This needs email verification: if the product signs new users in immediately, registration can't hide whether an email exists, so raise that tradeoff.
  • Password reset request: "If an account exists for this email, we've sent a reset link".
  • Rate limit: "Too many attempts. Wait a few minutes and try again".

Sign-in results show at the top of the form, in its status region, with the email kept. Field errors stay specific: "Enter your email address", "Use at least 15 characters", "This password is too common. Choose a different one", "This password has appeared in a data breach. Choose a different one", and "Passwords must match".

Sending

  • Validation runs first, with the Form Validation Pattern's timing.
  • While the request runs, the button has aria-disabled="true", ignores another press, and keeps focus, and the status region says "Signing in…". Don't disable the fields or the button: disabling the focused element drops focus to the page in Chromium and Firefox (checked).
  • The request has a time limit, 30 seconds suggested. A timeout or a dropped connection gets the network message, never the wrong-details one.
  • On success, go on to the app, or to the "Check your email" step. On failure, keep the email, show the message, and make the button work again.
// Sending the sign-in. The button keeps focus (aria-disabled, not disabled), a second submit // while one runs is ignored, and the status region says what's happening. Wrong details and // a failed connection get different messages, and neither says which field was wrong. // signIn() stands for the app's request and onSignedIn() for its next step; map the auth // service's answers to these messages. const form = document.getElementById('sign-in'); const button = form.querySelector('[type="submit"]'); const status = form.querySelector('[role="status"]'); const messages = {   401: 'Email or password is incorrect',   429: 'Too many attempts. Wait a few minutes and try again', };  form.addEventListener('submit', async (event) => {   event.preventDefault();   if (button.getAttribute('aria-disabled') === 'true') return;   button.setAttribute('aria-disabled', 'true');   status.textContent = 'Signing in…';   try {     const response = await signIn(new FormData(form), { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(30_000) });     if (response.ok) return onSignedIn(response);     status.textContent = messages[response.status] ?? 'Unable to sign in right now. Try again shortly';   } catch {     status.textContent = 'Unable to sign in right now. Try again shortly';   } finally {     button.removeAttribute('aria-disabled');   } });

Password managers, paste, and passkeys

  • autocomplete="username" on the email that identifies the account, also when it holds an email address; current-password at sign-in; new-password at registration and reset; and one-time-code on verification codes.
  • Never block paste or autofill (WCAG 2.2 3.3.8 Accessible Authentication).
  • Passkeys (optional): a "Sign in with a passkey" button, and passkey autofill with autocomplete="username webauthn" on the email field. If the prompt is cancelled or fails, focus returns to the passkey button, a short generic message shows, and the password form stays.

Accessibility

  • Labels are visible, and required and optional fields say so in words.
  • Field errors follow the Form Validation Pattern: text next to the field, aria-describedby and aria-invalid, and no live regions. A failed submit moves focus to the first invalid field.
  • One status region per form, for "Signing in…", the sign-in results, and the requirement status.
  • Buttons, Show password included, are at least 24 by 24 px (44 px suggested on touch), and text is at least 16 px on phones.

Layout and motion

These are suggested defaults; the project's design and tokens win.

  • A card at most 420 px wide, centered, with 48 px padding from 768 px wide and 24 px below.
  • On phones, the card fills the width minus 16 px gutters. Fields and buttons are 48 px tall.
  • Motion is optional: a 200 ms fade when switching forms. Under prefers-reduced-motion: reduce, changes are instant.

Edge cases

  • An email that already has an account: registration shows the same next step as for a new email, and the backend emails the account's owner a sign-in or reset link instead.
  • An older account whose password is shorter than today's minimum still signs in; ask for a new password after sign-in only if the auth service requires it.
  • A password filled by a password manager or pasted is accepted.
  • Spaces and Unicode in a password are kept as typed, never trimmed.
  • Too many attempts: the generic rate-limit message, worded the same whether or not the account exists.
  • A passkey prompt cancelled or failed: the password form stays, and focus returns to the passkey button.
  • A request that never answers ends at the time limit with the network message, and pressing Sign in again retries.
  • A product that signs new users in immediately can't hide at registration whether an email has an account: raise that tradeoff with the user.
  • Long emails and names scroll inside their fields, and nothing is cut off.

Acceptance checklist

  • [ ] Each form posts (method="post"), so a form sent before its script runs never puts a password in the URL
  • [ ] Sign-in accepts any non-empty password; registration and reset apply the length, common-password, and breach rules, with no composition rules
  • [ ] Passwords of 64 or more characters, spaces, and Unicode are accepted as typed
  • [ ] The requirements indicator never says "strong" from length alone, and screen readers hear its status when it changes
  • [ ] A failed sign-in says "Email or password is incorrect", a network or service failure says "Unable to sign in right now", and the email stays filled in
  • [ ] Registration, password reset, and rate-limit messages read the same whether or not the account exists
  • [ ] Password managers can save and fill the credentials, and paste works in every field
  • [ ] Show password keeps its name and focus, shows its state with aria-pressed, and the password is hidden again when the form is sent or reset, or the page comes back
  • [ ] Password fields have spellcheck="false"
  • [ ] While signing in, the button keeps focus with aria-disabled, a second press sends nothing, and the status region says "Signing in…"
  • [ ] Field errors follow the Form Validation Pattern, and a failed submit moves focus to the first invalid field
  • [ ] Passkey sign-in, if offered, falls back to the password form when it's cancelled or fails
  • [ ] The forms work at 320 px wide, with 16 px text on phones
  • [ ] Styles come from the project's styling system and tokens

See also

  • Text Input Field: the email and password fields.
  • Select and Combobox: a country or a language in registration forms.
  • Button: Sign in, Show password, and link-style actions.
  • Form Validation Pattern: when field errors appear, and where focus goes when a form is submitted.

These are suggestions; the forms work with any components and auth service.
excerpt: Sign-in and registration forms that follow current NIST password guidance, never reveal whether an email has an account, work with password managers and passkeys, and keep passwords out of URLs, spell-check services, and plain view.

title: Toast Notifications (Accessible) with Queue System
body:
A non-blocking toast notification system for providing user feedback after actions. Features success, error, warning, and info variants with queue management, auto-dismiss timers, manual dismiss controls, keyboard navigation, and full screen reader support.

Structure Specification

Component Hierarchy

The toast system consists of a Toast Container (fixed-position wrapper) that holds multiple Toast Items. Each Toast contains an Icon (indicating variant type), Content area (with Title and optional Description), and Action Buttons (Dismiss button and optional action like Undo).

The system flows as: Application triggers toast → Toast Manager adds to queue → Container renders visible toasts → Toast auto-dismisses or user dismisses → Next toast in queue appears.

Detailed Component Specifications

1. Toast Container

Goal: Manage the display and lifecycle of multiple toast notifications without blocking user interaction.

Positioning Options:

  • top-right (default) - Most common, good for desktop apps
  • top-left - Alternative for right-to-left layouts
  • bottom-right - Less intrusive, good for long sessions
  • bottom-left - Alternative placement
  • top-center - High visibility, good for critical messages
  • bottom-center - Mobile-first, often used in mobile apps

Container Dimensions:

  • Desktop: 380px width, fixed position
  • Mobile: Full width minus 32px total margins (16px each side)
  • Gap between toasts: 12px vertical spacing
  • Max visible toasts: 3 (configurable, older toasts queue)
  • Distance from viewport edge: 20px

States:

  • position (enum, default: "top-right") - Container placement
  • maxVisible (number, default: 3) - Maximum toasts shown simultaneously
  • queue (array) - Pending toasts waiting to be displayed
  • pauseOnHover (boolean, default: true) - Pause auto-dismiss on mouse hover
  • pauseOnFocusWithin (boolean, default: true) - Pause when toast has focus

2. Toast Item Component

Anatomy Slots:

  • icon - Variant-specific icon (success checkmark, error X, warning triangle, info circle)
  • content - Text content area
  • title - Main message (required)
  • description - Optional secondary text
  • action - Optional action button (e.g., "Undo")
  • dismiss - Close/dismiss button (X icon)
  • progressBar - Optional visual timeout indicator

Dimensions:

  • Height: Auto-sizing, minimum 60px
  • Padding: 16px all sides
  • Border radius: 10px
  • Shadow: Medium elevation (comparable to modals)
  • Icon size: 22px
  • Dismiss button size: 32×32px touch target
  • Progress bar height: 3px (if enabled)

Visual States:

  • variant (enum: "success" | "error" | "warning" | "info") - Visual style and semantics
  • visible (boolean) - Display state (controls enter/exit animations)
  • paused (boolean) - Whether auto-dismiss timer is paused
  • action (object, optional) - Action button config {label, onClick}

Color Variants:

Success:

  • Background: Green 50-100 (light), Green 900 (dark)
  • Border: Green 200-300 (light), Green 700 (dark)
  • Icon/Text: Green 600-700 (light), Green 100 (dark)
  • Icon: Checkmark circle

Error:

  • Background: Red 50-100 (light), Red 900 (dark)
  • Border: Red 200-300 (light), Red 700 (dark)
  • Icon/Text: Red 600-700 (light), Red 100 (dark)
  • Icon: X circle or exclamation circle

Warning:

  • Background: Amber/Yellow 50-100 (light), Amber 900 (dark)
  • Border: Amber 200-300 (light), Amber 700 (dark)
  • Icon/Text: Amber 700-800 (light), Amber 100 (dark)
  • Icon: Warning triangle or exclamation triangle

Info:

  • Background: Blue 50-100 (light), Blue 900 (dark)
  • Border: Blue 200-300 (light), Blue 700 (dark)
  • Icon/Text: Blue 600-700 (light), Blue 100 (dark)
  • Icon: Info circle or "i" icon

3. Toast Manager (State Management)

Core Responsibilities:

  • Queue management (add, remove, reorder toasts)
  • Auto-dismiss timers (start, pause, resume, cancel)
  • Maximum visible enforcement (hide overflow, show on dismiss)
  • Unique ID generation for each toast
  • Global toast API (show, dismiss, dismissAll methods)

State Variables:

toasts: Array<Toast> - id: string (unique identifier) - variant: "success" | "error" | "warning" | "info" - title: string - description?: string - duration: number (ms, 0 = persistent) - action?: {label: string, onClick: Function} - dismissible: boolean - timestamp: number (creation time) - paused: boolean  queue: Array<ToastConfig> - Pending toasts waiting for available slot  timers: Map<id, TimeoutID> - Active auto-dismiss timers by toast ID

API Methods:

  • toast.success(title, options?) - Show success toast
  • toast.error(title, options?) - Show error toast
  • toast.warning(title, options?) - Show warning toast
  • toast.info(title, options?) - Show info toast
  • toast.custom(config) - Show custom toast
  • toast.dismiss(id) - Dismiss specific toast
  • toast.dismissAll() - Clear all toasts
  • toast.promise(promise, messages) - Show loading → success/error based on promise result

4. Auto-Dismiss Behavior

Default Durations (configurable):

  • Success: 4000ms (4 seconds)
  • Info: 5000ms (5 seconds)
  • Warning: 6000ms (6 seconds)
  • Error: 7000ms (7 seconds) - Longer for critical messages
  • Persistent: 0ms (requires manual dismiss)

Timer Behavior:

  • Timer starts when toast becomes visible
  • Timer pauses on hover (if pauseOnHover=true)
  • Timer pauses when toast or action button has keyboard focus
  • Timer resumes when hover/focus ends
  • Timer resets if user interacts with action button
  • Timer cancelled on manual dismiss

Progress Bar (optional visual indicator):

  • Thin bar (2-4px height) at bottom or top of toast
  • Fills from 0% to 100% over duration period
  • Pauses fill when timer paused
  • Color matches variant accent color
  • Provides visual countdown for auto-dismiss

5. Queue System

Queue Rules:

  • Max visible toasts enforced (default: 3)
  • New toasts added to queue when limit reached
  • Oldest toast dismissed first when queue is full (FIFO)
  • Exception: High-priority toasts (error) can bump lower-priority
  • Queue processed on toast dismiss or timeout

Stacking Behavior:

  • Stack (default): Toasts stack vertically in container
  • Replace: New toast replaces previous toast (for rapid updates)
  • Queue: Toasts wait in queue until slot available

Position Ordering:

  • Top positions: Newest toast appears at top, pushes older down
  • Bottom positions: Newest toast appears at bottom, pushes older up
  • Animation: Slide in from edge, slide out on dismiss

Responsive Design

Desktop (≥1024px)

  • Fixed width: 380px
  • Positioned in corner (top-right default)
  • Multiple toasts stack vertically (max visible: 3-5)
  • Hover interactions enabled

Tablet (768px - 1023px)

  • Width: 360px
  • Positioned similar to desktop
  • Touch-friendly dismiss buttons (larger targets)
  • Max visible: 2-3 toasts

Mobile (<768px)

  • Full width minus 32px total margins (16px each side)
  • Positioned at bottom-center (recommended for mobile)
  • Swipe to dismiss gesture enabled (optional)
  • Single toast visible at a time (maxVisible: 1)
  • Touch targets: 44×44px minimum for all buttons

Accessibility

Keyboard Navigation

Focusable Elements:

  • Dismiss button (X): Always focusable
  • Action button (e.g., Undo): Focusable when present
  • Toast container: Not directly focusable

Keyboard Controls:

  • Escape: Dismiss focused toast (or all toasts if none focused)
  • Tab: Navigate between action and dismiss buttons within toast
  • Enter/Space: Activate focused button
  • Shift+Tab: Navigate backwards

Focus Management:

  • Newly appeared toasts do NOT steal focus (non-intrusive)
  • Keyboard users can Tab to reach toasts
  • Focus returns to trigger element on dismiss (if applicable)
  • Multiple toasts: Tab order follows visual stacking order

Screen Reader Support

ARIA Attributes:

  • Container: aria-live="polite" or aria-live="assertive" (for errors)
  • Toast: role="status" (success, info) or role="alert" (error, warning)
  • Title: aria-atomic="true" (announces full message)
  • Dismiss button: aria-label="Dismiss notification" or aria-label="Dismiss [variant] notification"
  • Action button: Descriptive label (e.g., aria-label="Undo delete action")

Announcement Strategy:

  • Success/Info: Polite announcements (don't interrupt)
  • Error/Warning: Assertive announcements (interrupt current speech)
  • Title + description read together
  • Multiple rapid toasts: Queue announcements to avoid overlap

Reduced Motion:

  • Disable slide/fade animations when prefers-reduced-motion: reduce
  • Use instant show/hide or simple fade
  • Maintain functionality without animations

Animations

Entry Animation

  • Slide in from container edge + fade in
  • Duration: 250ms
  • Easing: cubic-bezier(0.16, 1, 0.3, 1) (ease-out bounce)
  • Transform: translateX(100%) or translateY(-100%) → translate(0)
  • Opacity: 0 → 1

Exit Animation

  • Slide out to edge + fade out + scale down slightly
  • Duration: 200ms
  • Easing: cubic-bezier(0.4, 0, 1, 1) (ease-in)
  • Transform: translate(0) → translateX(100%) or translateY(-100%)
  • Opacity: 1 → 0
  • Scale: 1 → 0.95

Stacking Animation (Critical Implementation)

  • When toast dismissed, remaining toasts slide to fill gap
  • Duration: 200ms
  • Easing: cubic-bezier(0.4, 0, 0.2, 1) (standard ease)
  • CRITICAL - Coordinated Animation: Exit animation and stack repositioning happen SIMULTANEOUSLY
    • Exiting toast slides out WHILE remaining toasts smoothly slide up to fill the gap
    • No jumping or instant repositioning

Recommended Implementation Pattern (Wrapper Approach):

  • Use a wrapper element around each toast that handles height collapse
  • Structure: Wrapper (handles height/margin) → Toast (handles slide animation)
  • When exiting:
    • Wrapper animates: max-height from current to 0px AND margin-bottom from 12px to 0px (200-250ms)
    • Inner toast animates: translateX and opacity for slide out effect (200-250ms)
    • Both animations run simultaneously with same duration
  • Why: Wrapper stays in layout flow and collapses smoothly, allowing remaining toasts to slide up naturally without jumping
  • Common mistake: Setting position: absolute on toast directly causes it to jump to wrong position before animating

Progress Bar Animation

  • Linear progression from 0% to 100%
  • Duration: Matches auto-dismiss duration
  • Pause animation on hover/focus
  • Resume from current position when unpaused

Hover/Focus States

  • Dismiss button: Scale 1 → 1.1 on hover
  • Toast: Subtle elevation increase (shadow grows)
  • Action button: Background color shift
  • All transitions: 150ms ease-in-out

Usage Patterns

Basic Usage

// Success feedback toast.success("Changes saved successfully")  // Error feedback toast.error("Failed to delete item", {   description: "Please try again or contact support." })  // Warning with action toast.warning("Your session will expire in 5 minutes", {   action: {     label: "Extend",     onClick: () => extendSession()   } })  // Info notification toast.info("New version available", {   duration: 0, // Persistent until dismissed   action: {     label: "Reload",     onClick: () => window.location.reload()   } })

Promise-Based Usage

toast.promise(   saveData(),   {     loading: "Saving changes...",     success: "Changes saved!",     error: "Failed to save changes"   } )

Undo Pattern

toast.success("Item deleted", {   duration: 5000,   action: {     label: "Undo",     onClick: () => {       restoreItem()       toast.dismiss() // Close this toast     }   } })

Custom Configuration

toast.custom({   variant: "success",   title: "Profile updated",   description: "Your changes are now visible to others",   duration: 4000,   position: "bottom-center",   dismissible: true,   pauseOnHover: true })

State Management Integration

Context/Provider Pattern (React/Vue)

  • ToastProvider wraps application root
  • useToast hook provides toast methods
  • Central state management for all toasts

Global Singleton Pattern

  • Exported toast object with methods
  • Works across any component
  • No provider required

Event-Based Pattern

  • Dispatch custom events for toast actions
  • Toast container listens for events
  • Framework-agnostic approach

Testing Checklist

  • [ ] Success/error/warning/info variants display correct colors and icons
  • [ ] Toasts appear in correct container position (top-right, bottom-center, etc.)
  • [ ] Auto-dismiss works with correct durations (success: 4s, error: 7s, warning: 6s, info: 5s)
  • [ ] Manual dismiss (X button) removes toast with smooth exit animation
  • [ ] CRITICAL: Create 3 toasts, dismiss the MIDDLE one - it should slide out smoothly WITHOUT jumping to a different position first
  • [ ] CRITICAL: When middle toast exits, bottom toast should smoothly slide up (not jump instantly)
  • [ ] CRITICAL: Exit animation and stack repositioning happen simultaneously (coordinated animation)
  • [ ] Exit animation (200ms) and stack repositioning (200ms) run in parallel, not sequentially
  • [ ] Hover pauses auto-dismiss timer (if pauseOnHover enabled)
  • [ ] Keyboard focus pauses auto-dismiss timer (if pauseOnFocusWithin enabled)
  • [ ] Timer resumes when hover/focus ends
  • [ ] Queue enforces maxVisible limit (default: 3 toasts visible)
  • [ ] New toasts added to queue when maxVisible reached
  • [ ] Oldest toast dismissed first when queue is full (FIFO)
  • [ ] Queue processed correctly when toast dismissed or times out
  • [ ] Multiple toasts stack vertically with 12px spacing
  • [ ] Toasts slide to fill gap when one dismissed (stack animation)
  • [ ] Escape key dismisses focused toast or all toasts if none focused
  • [ ] Tab key navigates between action button and dismiss button
  • [ ] Enter/Space activates focused button
  • [ ] Focus order follows visual stacking order for multiple toasts
  • [ ] Screen reader announces new toasts with correct role (status/alert)
  • [ ] aria-live region configured correctly (polite for success/info, assertive for error/warning)
  • [ ] Title and description read together atomically by screen readers
  • [ ] Dismiss button has descriptive aria-label
  • [ ] Action button has descriptive aria-label (if present)
  • [ ] Entry animation: Slide in from edge + fade in (250ms)
  • [ ] Exit animation: Slide out to edge + fade out + slight scale down (200ms)
  • [ ] prefers-reduced-motion disables slide/scale animations, uses simple fade or instant
  • [ ] Progress bar (if enabled) animates from 0-100% over duration
  • [ ] Progress bar pauses when timer paused
  • [ ] Action button executes onClick callback
  • [ ] Action button optionally dismisses toast after callback
  • [ ] Mobile: Toasts are full width minus 32px margins
  • [ ] Mobile: Position switches to bottom-center (recommended)
  • [ ] Mobile: Touch targets are 44×44px minimum for buttons
  • [ ] Mobile: Only 1 toast visible at a time (maxVisible: 1)
  • [ ] Tablet: Toasts are 360px wide with touch-friendly buttons
  • [ ] Desktop: Toasts are 380px wide at configured position
  • [ ] Dark mode: Colors adapt with sufficient contrast for all variants
  • [ ] Rapid toast creation doesn't cause performance issues or queue overflow
  • [ ] toast.dismissAll() clears all active toasts and queue
  • [ ] Toast IDs are unique across all toasts
  • [ ] Timers cleaned up on unmount/dismiss (no memory leaks)
  • [ ] Container z-index (9999) places toasts above most UI but below modals
  • [ ] Long titles/descriptions wrap properly without truncation
  • [ ] Toast height adjusts automatically based on content length

Common Variations

Toast with Loading State

Show spinner in toast while async operation completes, then update to success/error.

Toast with Custom Icon

Allow custom icon instead of variant defaults (e.g., user avatar, custom SVG).

Toast with Rich Content

Support for custom content beyond title/description (e.g., images, links, formatted text).

Toast with Multi-Action

Multiple action buttons (e.g., "Save" and "Discard").

Notification Center Integration

Archive dismissed toasts in a notification center for later review.

Grouped Toasts

Combine similar toasts (e.g., "3 items deleted" instead of 3 separate toasts).

Framework Patterns

React

  • Context + useToast hook for global access
  • Custom hooks: useToastTimer, useToastQueue, useToastState
  • Portal for rendering outside DOM hierarchy (ReactDOM.createPortal)
  • useReducer or useState for toast state
  • Animations: Use react-transition-group or Framer Motion with AnimatePresence
  • Wrapper pattern recommended: Outer div handles height collapse, inner div handles slide animation

Vue

  • Composition API with provide/inject or Pinia store
  • Composable: useToast(), useToastTimer, useToastQueue, useToastState
  • Teleport for rendering in body (<Teleport to="body">)
  • ref/reactive for toast state
  • Animations: Use <TransitionGroup name="toast-list"> - Vue automatically handles move transitions
  • Important: Set position: absolute on .toast-list-leave-active to remove from layout during exit

Angular

  • Injectable ToastService with BehaviorSubject
  • Services: ToastService, ToastQueueService, ToastTimerService
  • Portal from @angular/cdk for rendering
  • BehaviorSubject for toast state
  • Animations: Use Angular animations with :enter, :leave, and query/stagger for move

Svelte

  • Writable stores for global toast state
  • Stores: toastStore, queueStore, toastAPI
  • Transition directives for animations (fly, fade, flip)
  • Portal pattern for rendering
  • Example: import { toast } from './toast'; toast.success('Saved!');

Edge Cases & Considerations

Rapid Toast Creation

  • Debounce identical messages within short timeframe (e.g., 500ms)
  • Group similar toasts (e.g., "3 items deleted")
  • Prevent queue overflow (max queue size: 10-20)

Long Messages

  • Wrap text properly (don't truncate)
  • Auto-adjust height based on content
  • Limit max height and add scroll if needed

Multiple Actions

  • Support secondary action button
  • Ensure proper keyboard navigation between multiple buttons
  • Consider toast width for multiple actions

Network State Changes

  • Offline toast: Persistent, high priority
  • Online toast: Brief success notification
  • Automatic toast on connection changes

Cleanup on Route Changes

  • Optionally dismiss all toasts on navigation
  • Or persist across routes for important messages
  • Configurable behavior per toast

Z-Index Conflicts

  • Toast container should be above most UI (z-index: 9999 or similar)
  • Below modals/dialogs if both open
  • Above dropdowns, tooltips, popovers

Performance

  • Limit DOM nodes (max visible + small queue)
  • Use CSS transforms for animations (hardware accelerated)
  • Debounce rapid updates
  • Clean up timers and event listeners

This toast notification system provides comprehensive user feedback while maintaining accessibility, performance, and a polished user experience across all devices and contexts.
excerpt: A non-blocking toast notification system with success/error/warning/info variants, queue management, auto-dismiss, keyboard navigation, and screen reader announcements. Perfect for user feedback after actions.

title: Text Input Field
body:
Most forms succeed or fail in their text fields: people need to know what to enter, whether they have to, and what went wrong. This guide covers single-line inputs and multi-line text areas, built on the native <input> and <textarea>, and targets WCAG 2.2 AA.

Start from what the project has

  1. If the project has a text field component, in its design system or a library it already uses, configure or extend it to meet this guide. Keep its API.
  2. Otherwise use the native <input> with the type that matches the data, or <textarea> for more than one line, with a <label>.

Implement only what the task needs, and add no dependency without asking. The project's conventions win for styling and visual defaults. If one conflicts with an accessibility or correctness requirement here, ask instead of choosing.

Structure

  • Label: visible text in a <label for> that names the field. A placeholder is never the label.
  • Hint (optional): short help, such as the format or why the field is asked for.
  • Input: <input> or <textarea>.
  • Error: an element that's empty and hidden until there's an error.
  • Count (optional): for fields with a length limit.
  • Leading icon (optional): decoration, with aria-hidden="true".
  • Trailing button (optional): such as Clear or Show password, a real <button type="button"> with a name, at least 24 by 24 px (44 px suggested on touch).

Labels, hints, and required fields

  • The label is visible, and its text is the field's accessible name. A native <label for> is enough; use aria-labelledby only when the name has to come from elsewhere.
  • Say "required" or "optional" in words. When most fields are required, mark the optional ones "(optional)", and say so once at the top of the form: "All fields are required unless marked (optional)". If the design uses an asterisk, explain it at the top of the form, and don't color it like an error.
  • Put the native required attribute on required fields: screen readers announce it, and the form's validation reads it. When the app shows its own error messages, the form gets novalidate (see the Form Validation Pattern).
  • Hints are text below the label or the field, connected with aria-describedby. A placeholder disappears as soon as someone types, so it never holds the format or instructions. A placeholder that shows anything needed meets 4.5:1.

Errors

  • An error says what's wrong and how to fix it, such as "Enter an email address in the correct format, like name@example.com", in text next to the field, with an icon if the design uses one.
  • The error element stays in the field's aria-describedby, after the hint. With no error it's empty and hidden, so it adds nothing. While there's an error, the field has aria-invalid="true".
  • Field errors are never live regions (role="alert" or aria-live): on a submit, every field would announce at once. When errors are announced and where focus goes is the form's job (see the Form Validation Pattern).
  • Keep what the person typed; never clear a field because it's wrong.

The snippets in this guide are plain HTML and JavaScript; adapt them to the project's framework and its version.

<p>All fields are required unless marked (optional).</p> <div class="field">   <label for="email">Email address</label>   <input id="email" name="email" type="email" autocomplete="email" required     aria-describedby="email-hint email-error">   <p class="field-hint" id="email-hint">We'll send your receipt here.</p>   <p class="field-error" id="email-error" hidden></p> </div> <div class="field">   <label for="phone">Phone number (optional)</label>   <input id="phone" name="phone" type="tel" autocomplete="tel"     aria-describedby="phone-hint phone-error">   <p class="field-hint" id="phone-hint">Include the country code, for example +44 20 7946 0958.</p>   <p class="field-error" id="phone-error" hidden></p> </div> 
// Shows or clears a field's error. The error stays in aria-describedby, so it's read with the // field; cleared, it's empty and hidden and adds nothing. aria-invalid tells screen readers // that the value needs fixing. function setFieldError(input, message) {   const error = document.getElementById(`${input.id}-error`);   error.textContent = message;   error.hidden = !message;   if (message) input.setAttribute('aria-invalid', 'true');   else input.removeAttribute('aria-invalid'); }

Types, autocomplete, and paste

  • Use the type that matches the data: email, tel, url, search, or password. It brings the right phone keyboard, and email and url a format check.
  • Codes, card numbers, and IDs are type="text" with inputmode="numeric", and one-time codes add autocomplete="one-time-code". type="number" is for quantities.
  • Fields that ask for the person's own data get the matching autocomplete token (WCAG 1.3.5), such as name, email, tel, street-address, postal-code, or bday. Passwords get current-password at sign-in and new-password when one is created.
  • Never block paste or autofill. Password managers and copied codes depend on them (WCAG 2.2 3.3.8).
  • Text is at least 16 px on phones: iOS Safari zooms the page when a smaller field gets focus.

Variants

  • Search: type="search", named "Search" by a visible or visually hidden label. Chromium and Firefox clear a search field on Escape themselves; no other field clears on Escape, since that would lose typing, and inside a dialog Escape closes the dialog. Chromium and WebKit also draw their own clear button in search fields, so a custom Clear button means hiding theirs (::-webkit-search-cancel-button).
  • Password: type="password" with the right autocomplete, spellcheck="false", and paste allowed. A Show password button is a toggle: its name stays "Show password", aria-pressed gives its state, and focus stays on it. The password is hidden again when the form is sent. The Login & Registration Forms guide has the full pattern.
  • Multi-line: <textarea> with the same label, hint, and error. It can grow with its content (field-sizing: content where supported).
  • Read-only: readonly keeps the value focusable, selectable, and sent with the form. disabled removes it from the Tab order and the form data, so use it only for fields that really can't be used yet, and say why in text.
  • Success (optional): only for checks the person can't see, such as an available username, with text such as "Username available". Not a green border and check on every valid field.

Length limits

  • Don't use maxlength for a limit people can reach. It cuts longer typed or pasted text without a word (checked in Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit), and stops typing without saying why.
  • Show the limit up front ("You can enter up to 200 characters"), count as people type ("You have 12 characters left"), and let them go over ("You have 30 characters too many"). Over the limit, the field is invalid until it's shortened, and the server checks the limit again.
  • The visible count changes on every keystroke; screen readers hear it once typing pauses, through one status region.
  • Count characters the way the server does. The snippet counts code points, so an emoji counts as one.
  • The count and the validity also cover the text the page starts with, such as a saved bio, and the text a form reset puts back. A reset brings it back without an input event and without clearing custom validity, so the snippet updates after the reset event has finished, unless a listener cancelled the reset; neither is announced. After setting the text from script, run the same update.
<label for="bio">Short bio (optional)</label> <textarea id="bio" name="bio" rows="4" aria-describedby="bio-count"></textarea> <p class="field-count" id="bio-count">You can enter up to 200 characters</p> <p class="visually-hidden" id="bio-count-status" role="status"></p> 
// A character count that lets people go over the limit, so a paste is never cut short, and // says by how much. The visible count changes as they type, and the status region speaks // once typing pauses. Over the limit, the field is invalid until it's shortened; the server // checks the limit again. const field = document.getElementById('bio'); const count = document.getElementById('bio-count'); const status = document.getElementById('bio-count-status'); const limit = 200; const characters = (n) => `${n} ${n === 1 ? 'character' : 'characters'}`; let pause;  // The count and the validity for the text as it is; call it again after setting the text // from script function update() {   const left = limit - [...field.value].length; // characters, not UTF-16 code units   if (field.value === '') count.textContent = `You can enter up to ${limit} characters`;   else count.textContent = left >= 0 ? `You have ${characters(left)} left` : `You have ${characters(-left)} too many`;   field.setCustomValidity(left >= 0 ? '' : `Enter ${limit} characters or fewer`); }  field.addEventListener('input', () => {   update();   clearTimeout(pause);   pause = setTimeout(() => { status.textContent = count.textContent; }, 1000); }); // After a reset that wasn't cancelled, count the text the form put back, unannounced. The // text comes back only after the reset event, and a later listener can cancel the reset. field.form?.addEventListener('reset', (event) => setTimeout(() => {   if (event.defaultPrevented) return;   clearTimeout(pause);   update(); })); update(); // text the page starts with, such as a saved bio, counts too

Appearance

These are suggested defaults; the project's design and tokens win.

  • States: default, hover, focus, error, read-only, disabled, and the optional success.
  • The field's edge has at least 3:1 contrast against the background in every state, and so does the focus indicator (WCAG 1.4.11). For example, #6b7280 on white is 4.8:1, while the common #d1d5db is 1.5:1, too faint to find the field. Check the project's own colors.
  • The error state changes more than the color: it has its message, and an icon if the design uses one.
  • Focus shows with :focus-visible, an outline or a ring, and is never removed without a replacement.
  • Sizes: 44 px tall (36 px compact, 52 px large), 16 px text, and 14 px labels, hints, and errors.
  • A field fills its container and has no breakpoints of its own. At 320 px wide and at 200% text size, labels, hints, and errors wrap.
  • Motion is optional: a 150 ms transition on the border and the focus ring. Under prefers-reduced-motion: reduce, changes are instant.

Edge cases

  • Hint and error together: both stay visible, and both stay in aria-describedby, the hint first.
  • Errors from the server show in the same error element, set the same way, at the field they belong to.
  • Autofill: autofilled values count as typed, and the field stays readable in the browser's autofill style (:autofill).
  • Right-to-left: icons and trailing buttons use logical properties, such as padding-inline-start, so they mirror.

Acceptance checklist

  • [ ] Every field has a visible label that is its accessible name, and no placeholder stands in for a label or a hint
  • [ ] Required and optional fields say so in words, and required fields have the required attribute
  • [ ] A screen reader reads the hint with the field, and the error too when there is one, with the field marked invalid
  • [ ] Errors say how to fix the problem, keep what was typed, and aren't live regions
  • [ ] Fields that ask for the person's own data have the matching autocomplete token, and paste works in every field
  • [ ] Codes and card numbers use inputmode="numeric", not type="number"
  • [ ] A field with a length limit keeps everything typed or pasted, says how many characters are too many, and announces the count only when typing pauses
  • [ ] The count and the validity are right for text the page starts with, and after a form reset; a cancelled reset changes nothing
  • [ ] Escape clears no field except a search field, where the browser does it
  • [ ] A Show password button keeps its name and focus, shows its state with aria-pressed, and the password is hidden again when the form is sent
  • [ ] Field edges and the focus indicator have at least 3:1 contrast and text 4.5:1, in every state
  • [ ] Text is at least 16 px on phones, and nothing is cut off at 320 px wide or at 200% text size
  • [ ] Styles come from the project's styling system and tokens, like its other form controls

See also

  • Form Validation Pattern: when errors appear, and where focus goes when a form is submitted.
  • Select and Combobox: choices from a list, with the same label, hint, and error wiring.
  • Login & Registration Forms: email and password fields, and the full Show password pattern.

These are suggestions; the field works with any form setup.
excerpt: An accessible text field on the native input or textarea: a visible label, hint and error text read with the field, required and optional marked in words, autocomplete for personal data, and a character count that never cuts text off.

title: Tabs Component
body:
Tabs look simple, and most of their problems are in the parts that don't show: a tab list without a name, every tab in the Tab order, panels that are moved out of view instead of hidden, and pages with URLs dressed up as tabs. This guide follows the APG tabs pattern and targets WCAG 2.2 AA.

Start from what the project has

  1. If the project has a tabs component, in its design system or a library it already uses, configure or extend it to meet this guide. Keep its API.
  2. Otherwise build it from plain HTML: buttons with tab roles, and panels.

Implement only what the task needs, and add no dependency without asking. The project's conventions win for styling and visual defaults. If one conflicts with an accessibility or correctness requirement here, ask instead of choosing.

When to use tabs

  • Tabs switch between panels of related content in one place on a page, one panel at a time, such as a settings page's sections or a record's details and history.
  • When each tab is a page with its own URL, it's navigation: links with aria-current="page" on the current one, styled like tabs if the design wants it, never role="tab".
  • Content people compare side by side belongs together on the page, and a long form reads better as sections with headings.

Structure

  • The tab list (role="tablist") is named: aria-labelledby pointing to a visible heading, or aria-label. It holds only tabs.
  • Each tab is a <button> with role="tab", an id, aria-selected, and aria-controls pointing to its panel. Each panel has role="tabpanel" and aria-labelledby pointing to its tab. Vertical tabs put aria-orientation="vertical" on the list.
  • Only the selected tab's panel shows. The others have the hidden attribute, or aren't rendered; moving them out of view leaves them in the reading and Tab order.
  • A panel gets tabindex="0" when its first content isn't focusable, so Tab from the tab list reaches it (APG).
  • A tab's full label is its text. Long labels wrap, or the list scrolls; a title tooltip doesn't show on focus or on touch. A tab isn't a button to screen readers, so only the Button guide's styles carry over, not its semantics.

Keys

  • The tab list is one Tab stop: Tab enters it on the selected tab and leaves it for the panel. The Tab stop (tabindex="0") follows focus while it's in the list, and goes back to the selected tab when focus leaves. Otherwise, after the arrows move focus to a tab that isn't selected, such as a disabled one or any tab with manual activation, Tab lands on the selected tab instead of leaving the list.
  • Right and Left Arrow move between tabs, swapped in right-to-left text, and Down and Up in a vertical list. They wrap at the ends. Home and End go to the first and the last tab. Arrows of the other direction are left to the page.
  • With automatic activation, the default, the tab that gets focus is selected; use it when panels show at once. With manual activation, the arrows move focus, and Enter or Space selects the focused tab; use it when a panel takes time to load.
  • A disabled tab has aria-disabled="true". It gets focus with the arrows, so screen reader users learn it exists, but it's never selected, by keys or by clicks (APG). Its label can say why, such as "Team (Business plan)".

The snippets in this guide are plain HTML and JavaScript; adapt them to the project's framework and its version.

<h2 id="settings-title">Settings</h2> <div role="tablist" aria-labelledby="settings-title">   <button type="button" role="tab" id="tab-profile" aria-controls="panel-profile" aria-selected="true">Profile</button>   <button type="button" role="tab" id="tab-billing" aria-controls="panel-billing" aria-selected="false" tabindex="-1">Billing</button>   <button type="button" role="tab" id="tab-team" aria-controls="panel-team" aria-selected="false" tabindex="-1" aria-disabled="true">Team (Business plan)</button>   <button type="button" role="tab" id="tab-security" aria-controls="panel-security" aria-selected="false" tabindex="-1">Security</button> </div> <!-- tabindex="0" on a panel that starts with text, so Tab from the tab list reaches it --> <div role="tabpanel" id="panel-profile" aria-labelledby="tab-profile" tabindex="0">…</div> <div role="tabpanel" id="panel-billing" aria-labelledby="tab-billing" tabindex="0" hidden>…</div> <div role="tabpanel" id="panel-team" aria-labelledby="tab-team" tabindex="0" hidden>…</div> <div role="tabpanel" id="panel-security" aria-labelledby="tab-security" tabindex="0" hidden>…</div> 
// The tab list is one Tab stop. The arrow keys move between tabs (Left and Right swap in // right-to-left text; Up and Down move in a vertical list), Home and End go to the first and // last tab, and with automatic activation the tab that gets focus is selected. A disabled tab // gets focus, so screen reader users learn it exists, but it's never selected. const tablist = document.querySelector('[role="tablist"]'); const tabs = [...tablist.querySelectorAll('[role="tab"]')]; const automatic = tablist.dataset.activation !== 'manual'; const disabled = (tab) => tab.getAttribute('aria-disabled') === 'true'; const tabStop = (tab) => tabs.forEach((other) => { other.tabIndex = other === tab ? 0 : -1; });  function select(tab) {   for (const other of tabs) {     const selected = other === tab;     other.setAttribute('aria-selected', String(selected));     document.getElementById(other.getAttribute('aria-controls')).hidden = !selected;   }   tabStop(tab); } tablist.addEventListener('click', (event) => {   const tab = event.target.closest('[role="tab"]');   if (tab && !disabled(tab)) select(tab); }); tablist.addEventListener('keydown', (event) => {   const index = tabs.indexOf(document.activeElement);   const vertical = tablist.getAttribute('aria-orientation') === 'vertical';   const forward = vertical ? 'ArrowDown' : getComputedStyle(tablist).direction === 'rtl' ? 'ArrowLeft' : 'ArrowRight';   const back = vertical ? 'ArrowUp' : forward === 'ArrowLeft' ? 'ArrowRight' : 'ArrowLeft';   const target = { [forward]: index + 1, [back]: index - 1, Home: 0, End: tabs.length - 1 }[event.key];   if (target === undefined || index < 0) return;   event.preventDefault();   const tab = tabs[(target + tabs.length) % tabs.length];   tab.focus();   if (automatic && !disabled(tab)) select(tab); }); // The Tab stop follows focus in the list, so Tab always leaves it for the panel, even from a // tab that has focus but isn't selected; when focus leaves, it goes back to the selected tab tablist.addEventListener('focusin', (event) => tabStop(event.target)); tablist.addEventListener('focusout', (event) => {   if (!tablist.contains(event.relatedTarget)) tabStop(tabs.find((tab) => tab.getAttribute('aria-selected') === 'true')); });

Panels that load

A panel whose content loads: select its tab at once and show the loading state in the panel. If people move on before it arrives, only the latest selection's answer fills its panel; number the requests, or abort the previous one. An error shows in the panel, with Retry. For panels that are always slow, use manual activation or load the likely ones ahead.

Many tabs

  • Fewer, shorter labels come first, then grouping tabs into higher-level sections.
  • A scrollable tab list scrolls sideways and keeps the selected tab in view. The arrow keys reach every tab, so Previous and Next scroll buttons, if any, sit next to the list, never inside it, and can stay out of the Tab order (tabindex="-1") and hidden from screen readers (aria-hidden="true").
  • Optional: a More button next to the list, for tabs that don't fit. It's a disclosure with a list of buttons, one per hidden tab; choosing one selects that tab and shows it in the row.

Adding and removing tabs

  • When a tab is removed and it had focus, focus moves to its neighbor, the next tab or else the previous one; otherwise focus stays where it is. A selected tab that's removed or becomes disabled hands the selection to its nearest enabled neighbor.
  • Optional: keep the selected tab in the URL, as a query parameter, so a reload or a shared link opens the same tab.

Phones

On phones, tabs are horizontal and scroll when their labels don't fit, and targets are 44 px tall; vertical tabs turn horizontal, or into sections with headings. Nothing scrolls sideways at 320 px wide apart from the tab list itself.

Appearance

These are suggested defaults; the project's design and tokens win.

  • Tabs are at least 44 px tall, with 12 to 16 px of padding on each side.
  • The selected tab is marked by more than color: an indicator line 2 to 3 px thick with 3:1 contrast against the background, and a stronger font weight. Focus indicators meet 3:1, and labels 4.5:1, disabled ones included. Check the project's own colors.
  • Motion is optional: the indicator moves over 180 ms, and a panel fades in over 150 ms. Under prefers-reduced-motion: reduce, nothing moves.

Edge cases

  • One tab: show the panel without a tab list.
  • Tabs inside a tab panel: avoid them; use headings or a second level of navigation.
  • Narrow containers: in a card or a grid cell, the tab list scrolls inside its container, and the panel never overflows it.

Acceptance checklist

  • [ ] The tab list is named by its heading or by aria-label, and holds only tabs
  • [ ] Each tab has role="tab", aria-selected, and aria-controls; each panel has role="tabpanel" and aria-labelledby
  • [ ] The tab list is one Tab stop: Tab enters it on the selected tab, and leaves it for the panel from any tab, even one that has focus but isn't selected; the panel has tabindex="0" when it starts with text
  • [ ] The arrow keys move between tabs and wrap at the ends, Home and End go to the first and last, and Left and Right swap in right-to-left text
  • [ ] Vertical tabs have aria-orientation="vertical" and use Up and Down; the other arrows are left to the page
  • [ ] With automatic activation the focused tab is selected; with manual activation, Enter or Space selects it
  • [ ] A disabled tab has aria-disabled="true", gets focus with the arrows, and is never selected by keys or clicks
  • [ ] Panels that aren't selected are hidden, or not rendered, not only moved out of view
  • [ ] A panel that loads shows its loading state at once, and only the latest selection's answer fills it
  • [ ] With many tabs, the list scrolls and keeps the selected tab in view, and any scroll buttons sit outside the tab list
  • [ ] Removing the focused tab moves focus to its neighbor; removing another tab leaves focus where it is
  • [ ] Pages with their own URLs use links with aria-current="page", not tabs
  • [ ] The selected tab is marked by more than color, and under reduced motion nothing moves
  • [ ] Styles come from the project's styling system and tokens

See also

  • Data Table (Sortable, Paginated, Filterable): views of a table, such as All, Open, and Archived, in tab panels.
  • Dashboard Layout with Collapsible Sidebar: dense admin pages split into panels.
  • Button: the project's button styles for tabs; a tab keeps role="tab".

These are suggestions; tabs work on their own.
excerpt: Tabs that switch panels in place, after the APG pattern: a named tab list that is one Tab stop, the arrow keys with Home and End, automatic or manual activation, and disabled tabs that can still be found.

title: Sidebar Navigation
body:
A sidebar holds an app's main sections, often in groups and nested lists, and many apps let people collapse it to a column of icons. The usual problems are in that rail: links that lose their names, a saved state that makes the page jump on every load, and a mobile copy of the sidebar with duplicate ids. This guide covers the sidebar, its rail, and its drawer on small screens, and targets WCAG 2.2 AA.

Start from what the project has

  1. If the project has a sidebar or navigation component, in its design system or a library it already uses, configure or extend it to meet this guide. Keep its API.
  2. Otherwise build it from plain HTML: a <nav> with lists of links, and buttons for groups.

Implement only what the task needs, and add no dependency without asking. The project's conventions win for styling and visual defaults. If one conflicts with an accessibility or correctness requirement here, ask instead of choosing.

Structure

  • The sidebar is a <nav> labelled for its purpose ("Main"). An <aside> can't take role="navigation", so the root is the <nav> itself.
  • Links sit in lists (<ul>), in groups under visible group labels; a nested list sits inside its parent's <li>. The DOM order is the order on screen, top to bottom, and so is the Tab order.
  • The current page's link has aria-current="page", marked by more than color: a bar at its edge with 3:1 contrast (WCAG 1.4.11), or a stronger background.
  • An item with children is a button with aria-expanded and aria-controls that shows its nested list; focus stays on it, and several groups can be open. A closed list is hidden (hidden, or display: none once a closing animation ends), so its links aren't in the Tab order; a list animated to height 0 alone keeps them there. An item with its own page and children needs two controls: the link, and a separate button for the list.
  • The group with the current page opens on load and on every route change, and the current link scrolls into view.
  • A badge's count is part of the link's text ("Orders 12 new"), visually hidden where the badge shows only "99+" or a dot. A plain <span> can't take an aria-label.
  • Leave out items the person can't use. One that has to show as unavailable for now is an <a> without href, with role="link", tabindex="0", and aria-disabled="true", so it's still found and does nothing; say why next to it. A link that opens a new tab says so.
  • When the sidebar comes before the main content, the page starts with a skip link to the main content (WCAG 2.4.1).

The collapsed rail

  • Suggested sizes: 260 px expanded, and a 64 px icon-only rail collapsed. An 80 px rail with a short label under each icon is an option; it helps people who don't know the icons or can't hover for a tooltip.
  • The rail is for 1024 px and wider, and so is its saved state: scope its styles to that width, as the snippet does. Below it, the sidebar is the drawer, always expanded, and the collapse toggle is hidden. Unscoped, a saved rail shrinks the drawer to 64 px and hides its labels.
  • The collapse toggle is a button whose name says what it does: "Collapse sidebar", then "Expand sidebar". Don't add aria-expanded to a name that changes, or it reads as a double state ("Collapse sidebar, expanded"); a stable name with aria-expanded is the other way. Focus stays on the toggle.
  • Collapsed, the labels are hidden visually only, so every link keeps its name; icons are aria-hidden. A badge shows as a dot on its icon, its number hidden visually the same way. If the dot has a ring to set it off from the icon, the ring takes the sidebar's background color; a white ring shows as a halo in dark mode.
  • Tooltips show the label on hover and on focus. They don't add aria-describedby: the name already has the label, so it would be read twice. They meet WCAG 1.4.13: Escape closes them, the pointer can move onto them, and they stay while the pointer or focus is on the link or the tooltip. Draw them in the top layer (the popover attribute), so the scrolling column doesn't clip them.
  • An item with children, pressed in the rail, expands the sidebar, as the toggle does, and opens its group, with focus kept on it. A search field shows as a search button that does the same and moves focus into the field.
  • Optional: hover expand. After a short delay (about 300 ms), the rail expands over the content while the pointer is on it, without moving the page, and collapses when the pointer leaves. Keyboard focus doesn't expand it; tooltips show the labels.

The snippets in this guide are plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript; adapt them to the project's framework and its version.

<nav class="sidebar" id="sidebar" aria-label="Main">   <ul>     <li>       <a href="/orders" aria-current="page">         <svg class="icon" aria-hidden="true"><use href="#icon-orders"></use></svg>         <span class="label">Orders</span>         <span class="badge">12<span class="visually-hidden"> new</span></span>       </a>     </li>     <li>       <a href="/customers">         <svg class="icon" aria-hidden="true"><use href="#icon-customers"></use></svg>         <span class="label">Customers</span>       </a>     </li>   </ul>   <button type="button" class="sidebar-toggle" aria-label="Collapse sidebar">     <svg class="icon" aria-hidden="true"><use href="#icon-chevron"></use></svg>   </button> </nav> 
.sidebar {   width: 260px; } .sidebar a {   position: relative; } /* The rail is for 1024 px and wider. Below that the sidebar is a drawer, always expanded,    whatever the saved state, so the rail's toggle goes too. */ @media (max-width: 1023.98px) {   .sidebar-toggle {     display: none;   } } @media (min-width: 1024px) {   [data-sidebar="collapsed"] .sidebar {     width: 64px;   }   /* Collapsed, the label and the badge's text are hidden visually only, so the link keeps its      name ("Orders 12 new"). A tooltip that shows the label adds nothing to the name. */   [data-sidebar="collapsed"] .sidebar :is(.label, .badge) {     clip-path: inset(50%);     height: 1px;     overflow: hidden;     position: absolute;     white-space: nowrap;     width: 1px;   }   /* In the rail, a badge shows as a dot on the icon */   [data-sidebar="collapsed"] .sidebar a:has(.badge)::after {     background: currentColor;     border-radius: 50%;     content: "";     height: 8px;     inset-inline-start: 34px;     position: absolute;     top: 6px;     width: 8px;   } }

Saving the collapsed state

  • Saving the collapsed state is optional. When the product saves it, keep it where the project keeps preferences: a cookie the server reads, so the server renders the right width, or storage under the app's own prefix (acme.sidebar, where acme stands for that prefix), applied by a small inline script in <head> before the first paint.
  • Reading it after hydration and hiding the jump with a fade still makes the sidebar jump on every page load for everyone who keeps it collapsed.
  • Storage can be blocked, so read and write it in try and catch; the sidebar then starts expanded, and the toggle still works on the page.
  • Where the framework renders <html> itself, as a Next.js root layout does, the attribute the script sets differs from the server's HTML, so tell the framework (React's suppressHydrationWarning on <html>).
<!-- In <head>, before the stylesheets render: apply the saved state, so the sidebar doesn't      jump. "acme" stands for the app's own storage prefix. --> <script>   try {     if (localStorage.getItem('acme.sidebar') === 'collapsed') {       document.documentElement.dataset.sidebar = 'collapsed';     }   } catch {     // Storage can be blocked; the sidebar then starts expanded   } </script> 
// The collapse toggle: its name says what it does, and the choice is saved for the next page const toggle = document.querySelector('.sidebar-toggle'); const root = document.documentElement;  function setCollapsed(collapsed) {   if (collapsed) root.dataset.sidebar = 'collapsed';   else delete root.dataset.sidebar;   toggle.setAttribute('aria-label', collapsed ? 'Expand sidebar' : 'Collapse sidebar'); } toggle.addEventListener('click', () => {   const collapsed = root.dataset.sidebar !== 'collapsed';   setCollapsed(collapsed);   try {     localStorage.setItem('acme.sidebar', collapsed ? 'collapsed' : 'expanded');   } catch {     // Not saved where storage is blocked; the choice still holds on this page   } }); setCollapsed(root.dataset.sidebar === 'collapsed'); // the name matches the saved state

Search

Optional: a labelled <input type="search"> ("Filter navigation") above the groups filters the links by their labels, opens the groups that have matches, and keeps the field in place when nothing matches. The number of matches goes to one polite status region once typing pauses ("3 links", "No links match"; WCAG 4.1.3).

The drawer on small screens

  • Below 1024 px, the same <nav> becomes a drawer, opened by a Menu button in the header. There's no second copy, so no id appears twice, and open groups and the search stay as they were.
  • While it's open, everything else on the page is inert (the Modal Dialog guide's model, without a focus-trap library), so focus and screen readers stay in it, and the page behind doesn't scroll. It makes inert only what isn't inert yet, and closing undoes only that, so a part of the page the app made inert stays inert. It shows expanded, whatever the saved state, 260 px wide or 85% of the window on phones.
  • It has a visible Close button ("Close menu"), because touch screen readers have no Escape key, and it also closes on Escape, on a click on the backdrop, and when a link in it is followed. Focus returns to the Menu button.
  • Closed, it's display: none; with a closing animation, it's inert from the moment closing starts.
  • If the window gets wider than 1024 px while it's open, it docks, the inertness it added goes, and focus on one of its links stays there, since it's the same element. When the window crosses 1024 px, focus on an element that hides moves to the nearest control that stays, and focus anywhere else stays where it is: widening hides the Menu button and Close, so focus on them, the drawer open or closed, moves to the current page's link, or to the first link that shows when that one is in a closed group, and narrowing hides the docked sidebar, so focus in it moves to the Menu button. React to a matchMedia change, not to resize events. Chromium drops focus from an element a media query hides before the listener runs, so remember the last focused element and check whether it still shows. The Dashboard Layout guide's drawer snippet shows this.

Layers

Layers, bottom to top: the page, sticky bars, dropdowns and popovers, toasts, then modals, which make the rest of the page inert. The project's layering scale wins; native <dialog> and the popover attribute use the top layer and need no z-index. The docked sidebar is page content, the drawer is a modal, and tooltips are popovers.

Appearance

These are suggested defaults; the project's design and tokens win.

  • Items are 40 px tall (44 px is comfortable for touch), icons 20 px, nested lists indented 16 px per level. Keep nesting to two or three levels.
  • Text meets 4.5:1, and the current item's marker and focus indicators 3:1. Check the project's own colors.
  • Labels wrap; nothing is cut off with an ellipsis.
  • Motion is optional: the width changes over 200 ms, and the drawer slides in over 250 ms. During the width change, overflow-x: hidden on the column and on its scrolling area stops a scrollbar from flashing. Under prefers-reduced-motion: reduce, nothing slides.

Edge cases

  • Deep nesting: past three levels, flatten the tree or move the deeper pages into their section's own navigation.
  • Many items: the column scrolls on its own, and the current link scrolls into view.
  • Right side and right-to-left: logical properties (inset-inline-start, margin-inline-start) put the sidebar and the drawer on the start side in right-to-left text, or on either side by choice.
  • With a top bar: the sidebar starts below it: its sticky top is the bar's height. The drawer covers both.
  • Before the script runs: render the links on the server, with the current group open.

Acceptance checklist

  • [ ] The sidebar is a nav labelled for its purpose, with its links in lists and aria-current="page" on the current one, marked by more than color
  • [ ] An item with children is a button with aria-expanded that shows its nested list, and a closed list is hidden, so its links are out of the Tab order
  • [ ] The group with the current page opens on load and on route changes, and its link scrolls into view
  • [ ] Collapsed to the rail, every link keeps its name (the label visually hidden, the icon aria-hidden), and a badge's count is in the link's name
  • [ ] Tooltips in the rail show on hover and on focus, close on Escape, can be hovered, and add no aria-describedby
  • [ ] In the rail, an item with children expands the sidebar and opens its group, with focus kept on it
  • [ ] The collapse toggle's name says what it does, focus stays on it, and the choice is saved under the app's own prefix
  • [ ] A saved collapsed state applies before the first paint, so the sidebar doesn't jump on load; with storage blocked it starts expanded
  • [ ] The search field's number of matches is said in one polite status region
  • [ ] Below 1024 px, the same nav opens as a drawer with a visible Close button; while it's open, the rest of the page is inert and doesn't scroll
  • [ ] Close, Escape, the backdrop, and a followed link close the drawer, focus returns to the Menu button, and what was inert before the drawer opened stays inert
  • [ ] Crossing 1024 px either way, focus on what hides moves to what stays: from the Menu button or Close to the current page's link (or the first link that shows, when that one is in a closed group), and from the sidebar to the Menu button; focus anywhere else stays where it is
  • [ ] The rail and its saved state apply from 1024 px only: the drawer is always expanded, without the collapse toggle
  • [ ] Labels wrap instead of being cut off, and under reduced motion nothing slides
  • [ ] Styles come from the project's styling system and tokens

See also

  • Dashboard Layout with Collapsible Sidebar: the app shell this sidebar docks into, with the drawer snippet.
  • Navigation Bar (Responsive) with Mobile Menu: a top bar next to the sidebar, with the same skip link and layering.
  • Command Palette: keyboard-first navigation to the same destinations.
  • Documentation Website Layout: a documentation site's page tree.
  • AI Agent Chat Layout: an AI chat whose conversation list sits next to the app's navigation.

These are suggestions; the sidebar works on its own.
excerpt: An app's side navigation: groups and nested lists, a collapsible icon rail that still names every link, a saved collapsed state that never jumps, and the same nav as a drawer on small screens.

title: Navigation Bar (Responsive) with Mobile Menu
body:
The navigation bar is on every page, so its mistakes repeat everywhere: a sticky bar that hides the focused link, dropdowns that trap focus or vanish, a mobile menu that leaves the page behind it reachable. This guide covers the bar, its dropdowns, its menu on small screens, and the app variant's account menu and notifications, and targets WCAG 2.2 AA.

Start from what the project has

  1. If the project has a header or navigation component, in its design system or a library it already uses, configure or extend it to meet this guide. Keep its API.
  2. Otherwise build it from plain HTML: a <header> with the skip link, the logo, a <nav> with the links, and the actions.

Implement only what the task needs, and add no dependency without asking. The project's conventions win for styling and visual defaults. If one conflicts with an accessibility or correctness requirement here, ask instead of choosing.

Structure

  • The bar is the page's <header>, its banner landmark. It starts with the skip link, then the logo, a link to the home page named with the site's name (the logo image's alt text), then a <nav> with the site's links, labelled "Main", then the actions.
  • The current page's link has aria-current="page" and looks different by more than color, such as an underline.
  • Leave out links the person can't use. One that has to show as unavailable for now is an <a> without href, with role="link", tabindex="0", and aria-disabled="true", so it's still found and does nothing; say why next to it.
  • A link that opens a new tab says so in its text, visible or visually hidden.
  • Variants: a marketing bar has links, dropdowns for groups of pages, and one call to action, which is a link when it goes to a page. An app bar has links, notifications, and the account menu (see "App bar" below), and stays solid.

Dropdowns

  • An item with children is a button that shows or hides its list of links, with aria-expanded and aria-controls. It has no aria-haspopup and no role="menu": those announce an app menu with arrow-key behavior, and these are links.
  • An item with its own page and children needs two controls: the link, and a separate button that shows the list, named after it ("More Products pages").
  • Focus stays on the button when the list opens, and Tab moves on into the list. One list is open at a time. A closed list has the hidden attribute, so its links aren't in the Tab order.
  • Escape closes the open list and puts focus back on its button. A click outside the navigation, or focus moving out of it, closes the list too. When focus goes nowhere (relatedTarget is null, as when macOS Safari doesn't focus a clicked link), the click decides, so a click on a link in the list still lands.
  • Lists open on a click, Enter, or Space, never on hover alone.
  • In a single-page app, close the list when one of its links is followed.

The snippets in this guide are plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript; adapt them to the project's framework and its version.

<nav class="site-nav" aria-label="Main">   <ul>     <li>       <button type="button" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="nav-products">Products</button>       <ul id="nav-products" hidden>         <li><a href="/analytics">Analytics</a></li>         <li><a href="/reports">Reports</a></li>       </ul>     </li>     <li>       <button type="button" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="nav-company">Company</button>       <ul id="nav-company" hidden>         <li><a href="/about">About</a></li>         <li><a href="/careers">Careers</a></li>       </ul>     </li>     <li><a href="/pricing" aria-current="page">Pricing</a></li>   </ul> </nav> 
// Disclosure dropdowns: each button shows or hides its own list of links, one list at a time. // A closed list is hidden, so its links aren't in the Tab order. const nav = document.querySelector('.site-nav'); const toggles = [...nav.querySelectorAll('button[aria-controls]')];  function setOpen(toggle, open) {   toggle.setAttribute('aria-expanded', String(open));   document.getElementById(toggle.getAttribute('aria-controls')).hidden = !open; } const closeAll = () => toggles.forEach((toggle) => setOpen(toggle, false));  for (const toggle of toggles) {   toggle.addEventListener('click', () => {     const open = toggle.getAttribute('aria-expanded') !== 'true';     closeAll();     setOpen(toggle, open);   }); } // Escape closes the open list and puts focus back on its button nav.addEventListener('keydown', (event) => {   const open = toggles.find((toggle) => toggle.getAttribute('aria-expanded') === 'true');   if (event.key !== 'Escape' || !open) return;   setOpen(open, false);   open.focus(); }); // Focus moving out of the navigation, or a click outside it, closes the list. When focus goes // nowhere (relatedTarget is null, as when Safari doesn't focus a clicked link), the click decides. nav.addEventListener('focusout', (event) => {   if (event.relatedTarget && !nav.contains(event.relatedTarget)) closeAll(); }); document.addEventListener('click', (event) => {   if (!nav.contains(event.target)) closeAll(); });

Sticky bar and skip link

  • position: sticky with top: 0 keeps the bar at the top without a script. Switching to position: fixed from a scroll handler makes the content jump up by the bar's height.
  • scroll-padding-top on the root element, set to the bar's height, makes the page scroll focused elements and link targets clear of the bar (WCAG 2.2 2.4.11). Without it, a link focused under the bar stays covered (checked in Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit). Where the bar's height changes, as on phones, set the value again; keep the bar to one line so its height holds.
  • The skip link is the first focusable element: "Skip to content", shown while it has focus, going to <main id="main" tabindex="-1"> (WCAG 2.4.1).
  • Optional, for marketing pages: the bar starts transparent over a hero and turns solid once the page scrolls. An IntersectionObserver on a small element at the top of the page switches it exactly at the threshold, with no scroll listener; the same observer can add a shadow. The bar's text meets 4.5:1 against what's behind it in both states, the hero image included. App bars stay solid.
<!-- The skip link is the header's first child, so it's the page's first Tab stop --> <header class="site-header">   <a class="skip-link" href="#main">Skip to content</a>   <a class="logo" href="/">Acme</a>   <!-- the site's <nav> --> </header> <main id="main" tabindex="-1">   <!-- the page --> </main> 
/* The bar stays at the top without a script, and the page scrolls focused elements and link    targets clear of it. Both use the bar's height; set it again where the height changes. */ :root {   --site-header-height: 60px; } @media (min-width: 1024px) {   :root {     --site-header-height: 72px;   } } html {   scroll-padding-top: var(--site-header-height); } .site-header {   position: sticky;   top: 0;   z-index: 10; /* the sticky-bar layer of the project's scale */   min-height: var(--site-header-height); } /* The skip link shows over the bar while it has focus */ .skip-link {   position: absolute;   inset-inline-start: 0.5rem;   top: 0.5rem; } .skip-link:not(:focus) {   clip-path: inset(50%);   height: 1px;   overflow: hidden;   white-space: nowrap;   width: 1px; }

The menu on small screens

  • Below 1024 px, the links and the actions move into a menu opened by a Menu button. It's one switch: from 1024 px the bar shows its links, below that the Menu button.
  • The menu is a native <dialog> opened with showModal(), named "Main menu". The browser makes the rest of the page inert, closes it on Escape, and returns focus to the Menu button (checked in Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit). Without a native dialog, follow the Modal Dialog guide's model: the rest of the page inert, and no focus-trap library.
  • It has a visible Close button ("Close menu"), and it also closes on a click on the backdrop and when a link in it is followed.
  • Inside it, an item with children is an accordion section: a button with aria-expanded that shows its links. Opening one doesn't close the menu, and several can be open.
  • The page behind doesn't scroll: overflow: hidden on the root element while the menu is open (html:has(dialog:modal)), with scrollbar-gutter: stable, so the page doesn't shift.
  • When the window crosses 1024 px, focus on an element that hides moves to the nearest control that stays, and focus anywhere else stays where it is. Widening with the menu open closes it and moves focus to the same link in the bar; widening with focus on the Menu button, which hides, moves focus to the current page's link in the bar. In both cases, when that link is in a closed dropdown list, focus goes to the first link in the bar that shows instead; narrowing with focus on the bar's links, which hide, moves focus to the Menu button. React to a matchMedia change, not to resize events. Chromium drops focus from an element a media query hides before the listener runs, so remember the last focused element and check whether it still shows.
  • The menu's copy of the links gets its own ids.

App bar: account and notifications

  • The account menu is a disclosure like the dropdowns: a button named "Account" (or the person's name) with aria-expanded, and a list of links. Sign out is a button that posts a form, not a link.
  • The notifications button's name includes the count ("Notifications, 3 unread"), and the badge is hidden from screen readers, since the name already says it. The badge isn't a live region; new notifications, if announced at all, go through one polite status region.

Layers

Layers, bottom to top: the page, sticky bars, dropdowns and popovers, toasts, then modals, which make the rest of the page inert. The project's layering scale wins; native <dialog> and the popover attribute use the top layer and need no z-index. The bar is a sticky bar: an open dropdown list sits above the page, and a modal dialog covers the bar.

Appearance

These are suggested defaults; the project's design and tokens win.

  • The bar is 72 px tall from 1024 px and 60 px below. Links are 16 px, and links and buttons are at least 24 px tall (44 px is comfortable for touch).
  • Text meets 4.5:1, and focus indicators and the current link's marker 3:1. A badge with white text needs a dark enough red: #dc2626 is 4.8:1, #ef4444 only 3.8:1. Check the project's own colors the same way.
  • Labels wrap; nothing is cut off with an ellipsis. At 320 px wide nothing scrolls sideways.
  • Motion is optional: a list fades in over 150 ms, and the menu slides in over 250 ms. Under prefers-reduced-motion: reduce, they appear without movement.

Edge cases

  • Many links: group them into dropdowns, or switch to the menu at a wider breakpoint, so the row never wraps under the bar.
  • Before the script runs: render the links on the server. A dropdown's parent can be a link to an overview page, so every page is reachable before the script runs.
  • Single-page apps: a route change closes an open list and the menu, and moves aria-current.
  • A missing return target: if the button that opened something is gone when it closes, move focus somewhere sensible nearby, such as the bar's first link, never the page's body.

Acceptance checklist
