  • [ ] The page starts with a "Skip to content" link that shows when it has focus and moves focus to the main area
  • [ ] The bar sticks to the top with CSS alone, and a link focused under it is scrolled clear of it (scroll-padding-top at the bar's height)
  • [ ] The bar is the page's header, its links are in a labelled nav, and the current page's link has aria-current="page"
  • [ ] Each dropdown is a button with aria-expanded and aria-controls and no aria-haspopup, and a closed list is hidden
  • [ ] Focus stays on the button when its list opens, Tab moves through the list's links, and one list is open at a time
  • [ ] Escape closes the open list and returns focus to its button; a click outside, or focus leaving the navigation, closes it too
  • [ ] Lists open on a click, Enter, or Space, never on hover alone
  • [ ] Below 1024 px, a Menu button opens the links in a native dialog named "Main menu", with a visible Close button
  • [ ] While the menu is open, the rest of the page is inert and doesn't scroll; Close, Escape, the backdrop, and a followed link close it, and focus returns to the Menu button
  • [ ] Crossing 1024 px either way, focus on what hides moves to what stays: from the menu or the Menu button to the bar's links when widening, and from the bar's links to the Menu button when narrowing; focus anywhere else stays where it is
  • [ ] The account menu is a disclosure with a Sign out button, and the notifications button's name includes the unread count
  • [ ] An open modal dialog covers the bar, and a transparent bar's text meets 4.5:1 over whatever is behind it
  • [ ] Labels wrap instead of being cut off, nothing scrolls sideways at 320 px wide, and under reduced motion nothing slides
  • [ ] Styles come from the project's styling system and tokens

See also

  • Modal Dialog: the model for a menu without a native dialog.
  • Command Palette: a search and command entry point in the bar, opened with Cmd or Ctrl+K.
  • Dashboard Layout with Collapsible Sidebar: an app shell whose header has the same account menu and notifications.
  • AI Agent Chat Layout: the header of an AI chat.

These are suggestions; the bar works on its own.
excerpt: A site's top bar with a skip link, links with disclosure dropdowns, and a menu in a native dialog on small screens. It sticks with CSS alone and keeps focused elements in view below it.

title: File Upload Component
body:
Attaching a file should work however people work: with a keyboard, a mouse, a touch screen, or by dragging from their desktop. This guide covers choosing and dropping files, checking them, and listing them with their progress and errors. It targets WCAG 2.2 AA.

Start from what the project has

  1. If the project has an upload component, library, or service, configure or extend it to meet this guide. Keep its API and its upload code.
  2. Otherwise build on the native <input type="file">: a visible button opens it, and the app keeps the chosen files and sends them.

Implement only what the task needs, and add no dependency without asking. The project's conventions win for styling and visual defaults. If one conflicts with an accessibility or correctness requirement here, ask instead of choosing.

Structure

  • Group: an element with role="group", named by the field's visible label (aria-labelledby). The whole group is the drop area. It isn't a button: interactive elements can't sit inside a button, and a drop area is a region, not a control.
  • Hint: what's accepted and the limits ("PDF or Word files, up to 10 MB each"), and that files can be dropped or chosen. It describes Choose files (aria-describedby).
  • Error: for the field as a whole, such as "Choose at least one file", also in Choose files' aria-describedby, empty and hidden until it's needed.
  • Choose files: a <button type="button"> that opens the picker by calling the hidden input's click(). It's the way in that needs no dragging (WCAG 2.2 2.5.7).
  • File input: type="file" with accept and multiple, hidden. accept filters the picker.
  • File list: each file's name as text, never HTML, its size, its status, its progress while uploading, and its buttons.
  • Status region: one, present before it changes, for files added, removed, rejected, uploaded, and failed.

The snippets in this guide are plain HTML and JavaScript; adapt them to the project's framework and its version.

<div class="upload" role="group" aria-labelledby="documents-label">   <p class="upload-label" id="documents-label">Documents (optional)</p>   <p class="upload-hint" id="documents-hint">PDF or Word files, up to 10 MB each. Drop them here, or choose them.</p>   <p class="upload-error" id="documents-error" hidden></p>   <button type="button" class="upload-choose" aria-describedby="documents-hint documents-error">Choose files</button>   <input type="file" id="documents" multiple accept=".pdf,.doc,.docx" hidden>   <ul class="upload-files" aria-label="Chosen files">     <!-- One item per file, its name set as text, never as HTML -->     <li>       <span class="upload-name">report.pdf</span>       <progress max="100" value="40" aria-label="Uploading report.pdf"></progress>       <button type="button">Remove <span class="visually-hidden">report.pdf</span></button>     </li>   </ul>   <p class="visually-hidden" role="status"></p> </div>

Choosing and dropping

  • Choose files opens the picker with a click, Enter, or Space.
  • Files dropped anywhere in the area are added. The area highlights while files are dragged over it; a counter keeps the highlight steady while the pointer crosses the elements inside, and drags of text or links don't highlight it.
  • A file dropped just outside the area would open in the tab and replace the page, form and all. While the uploader is on the page, cancel dragover and drop for files on the whole page.
  • After reading the chosen files, clear the input's value. Otherwise, choosing the same file again, for example after removing it, fires no change in Chrome and Safari.
  • Paste (optional): pasted files go through the same checks.
// Choosing and dropping files. The whole upload group takes dropped files, and a counter keeps // its highlight steady while the pointer crosses the elements inside it. addFiles(files) // stands for the app's own handling: check each file, list it, and start its upload. const area = document.querySelector('.upload'); const input = document.getElementById('documents'); const hasFiles = (event) => event.dataTransfer?.types.includes('Files'); let depth = 0;  area.querySelector('.upload-choose').addEventListener('click', () => input.click()); input.addEventListener('change', () => {   addFiles([...input.files]);   input.value = ''; // so choosing the same file again fires change again });  area.addEventListener('dragenter', (event) => {   if (!hasFiles(event)) return;   depth += 1;   area.classList.add('is-dragging'); }); area.addEventListener('dragleave', (event) => {   if (hasFiles(event) && --depth === 0) area.classList.remove('is-dragging'); }); area.addEventListener('drop', (event) => {   depth = 0;   area.classList.remove('is-dragging');   addFiles([...event.dataTransfer.files]); });  // A file dropped anywhere else on the page would open in the tab and replace it for (const type of ['dragover', 'drop']) {   window.addEventListener(type, (event) => {     if (hasFiles(event)) event.preventDefault();   }); }

Checking files

  • Check each file when it's added: its type against accept, its size, and the count. Reject it next to its name with the reason ("photo.heic isn't a PDF or Word file", "video.mp4 is larger than 10 MB"), and say it in the status region.
  • file.type is the browser's guess from the extension, and empty for types it doesn't know, so match accept against the extension too, ignoring case.
  • These checks are for the person's convenience. The server checks the type by the file's content, the size, and the count again, and treats file names as text.
  • With one file, a new choice replaces the current one, and the status region says so. With several, files are added up to the limit, and the status region says when it's reached.
  • A file with the same name, size, and modification time as one already chosen is ignored with a message, or replaces it; say which.
// Why a file can't be added, or null when it can: its type against the input's accept list, // its size, and how many files are already chosen. file.type is the browser's guess from the // extension, and empty for types it doesn't know, so extensions count too, in any case. The // server checks everything again, the type by the file's content. function rejection(file, { accept = '', maxBytes = Infinity, chosen = 0, maxFiles = Infinity } = {}) {   const name = file.name.toLowerCase();   const type = file.type.toLowerCase();   const rules = accept.split(',').map((rule) => rule.trim().toLowerCase()).filter(Boolean);   const typeAllowed = rules.length === 0 || rules.some((rule) => (     rule.startsWith('.') ? name.endsWith(rule)       : rule.endsWith('/*') ? type.startsWith(rule.slice(0, -1))         : type === rule));   if (!typeAllowed) return 'type';   if (file.size > maxBytes) return 'size';   if (chosen >= maxFiles) return 'count';   return null; }

The file list and uploads

  • Each file shows its name, size, and status: ready, uploading, uploaded, failed, cancelled, or unknown. Its buttons are Remove, and Cancel or Retry while they apply, each named after the file, with visually hidden text after the visible word ("Remove report.pdf").
  • Progress is the native <progress> element, named after its file. fetch() reports no upload progress, so use XMLHttpRequest's upload events, or the project's upload library.
  • Cancel aborts the request. Give each file an id (crypto.randomUUID()). A dropped connection leaves the outcome unknown, since the server may have the file: the status says so, and Retry sends the same id, so the server keeps one copy.
  • The status region says when each file is added, removed, uploaded, or fails ("report.pdf uploaded"), at meaningful moments, never every percent.
  • After Remove, focus moves to the next file's Remove button, or the previous one, or Choose files when the list is empty, never to the page body.
  • Image previews are optional: an <img> from URL.createObjectURL(), released with URL.revokeObjectURL() when the file is removed. An <img> doesn't run an SVG's scripts; a user's file never goes in an <iframe> or <object>.
  • Files sent with the form, rather than uploaded as they're added, are added to the form data by the app, since the input is cleared after each choice.
  • A form reset doesn't clear the app's list of chosen files, since the input is empty after each choice anyway. After a reset that wasn't cancelled, clear the list, cancel unfinished uploads, release preview URLs, and say so in the status region. Wait for the reset event to finish, and check defaultPrevented first: a later listener can still cancel the reset.

Accessibility

  • Everything works from the keyboard: Choose files, and each file's buttons. File rows aren't focusable, and there are no row shortcuts: Delete or Backspace on a row would need a Tab stop per file, and the Remove button is enough.
  • The hint says that files can be dropped, so the highlight isn't the only cue.
  • A required upload says so in words. A submit without a file shows the field's error, and focus moves to Choose files.
  • Text meets 4.5:1, and the area's edge, the highlight, and the focus indicator 3:1. Buttons are at least 24 by 24 px (44 px suggested on touch).

Layout and motion

These are suggested defaults; the project's design and tokens win.

  • The area fills its container and is at least 96 px tall. On phones, the list is one column, with each file's buttons at the end of its row; thumbnails are optional.
  • At 320 px wide, long file names wrap, and nothing scrolls sideways.
  • Motion is optional: the highlight fades in over about 140 ms, and new files over 160 ms. Under prefers-reduced-motion: reduce, nothing moves, and the progress element still fills.

Edge cases

  • Long file names wrap, or are shortened in the middle with the full name kept in the item's text for screen readers.
  • Leaving during uploads: warn before the page is left (beforeunload) while uploads run, or let them finish in the background if the app can.
  • When the upload can't be used yet: say why in text, and give Choose files aria-disabled="true", so it can still be found.
  • Files the server rejects show its message next to the file, with Remove.

Acceptance checklist

  • [ ] Choose files opens the picker with a click, Enter, or Space, so nothing needs dragging
  • [ ] Files dropped anywhere in the area are added, and a file dropped elsewhere on the page doesn't open in the tab
  • [ ] The highlight shows only while files are dragged over the area, and doesn't flicker over the elements inside it
  • [ ] The same file can be chosen again after it was removed
  • [ ] Each file is checked against the accepted types, with extensions in any case, the size, and the count, and a rejected file says why, by name
  • [ ] The server checks the type by content, the size, and the count again, and file names are shown as text
  • [ ] Each file's Remove, Retry, and Cancel buttons are named after it, and its progress is a progress element named after it
  • [ ] One status region announces files added, removed, uploaded, and failed, without announcing every percent
  • [ ] After Remove, focus lands on another file's Remove button or on Choose files, never on the page body
  • [ ] A dropped connection shows the upload's outcome as unknown, and Retry doesn't create a second copy
  • [ ] A form reset clears the list of chosen files and cancels unfinished uploads, and a cancelled reset changes nothing
  • [ ] The area's edge, its text, and the focus indicator meet the contrast minimums, and buttons are at least 24 by 24 px
  • [ ] Styles come from the project's styling system and tokens, like its other form controls

See also

  • Form Validation Pattern: required uploads, and errors when a form is submitted.
  • Select and Combobox: the other fields in upload and settings forms.
  • Login & Registration Forms: registration and profile forms that ask for a photo or a document.

These are suggestions; the upload works in any form.
excerpt: A file upload that works by keyboard, pointer, and drag and drop: a button opens the picker, the whole area takes dropped files without the browser opening them, and each file is checked and listed with its own progress and Remove button, while the server checks everything again.

title: Select and Combobox
body:
People choose from lists everywhere in forms. The browser's <select> already does this well, so a custom list is only worth building when it needs search, several choices, or richer options. This guide covers both, and targets WCAG 2.2 AA.

Start from what the project has

  1. If the project has a select or combobox component, in its design system or a library it already uses, configure or extend it to meet this guide. Keep its API.
  2. Otherwise choose by what the list needs:
    • One choice, no search: the native <select>. Every screen reader knows it, and phones open their own picker.
    • Search, a long list, or results from the server: a combobox after the APG pattern, a text input with role="combobox" that filters a list.
    • Several choices: the same combobox with a multi-select list, and the chosen values shown outside the input.
    • Rich options without search, such as icons or two lines: the APG select-only combobox, with its own keys (see "Rich options without search" below). Where the native select only needs custom styling, appearance: base-select styles it in Chromium (from Chrome 135); other browsers show the standard select.

Implement only what the task needs, and add no dependency without asking. The project's conventions win for styling and visual defaults. If one conflicts with an accessibility or correctness requirement here, ask instead of choosing.

The native select

  • Give it a <label for>, required when a choice is needed, and autocomplete for personal data, such as country or bday-month.
  • For required to work, the first option is a placeholder with value="", such as "Choose a country". A placeholder without value="" counts as a choice, so the form accepts it (checked in Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit).
  • Group options with <optgroup label>.
  • Choosing an option doesn't change the page by itself (WCAG 3.2.2); the choice applies when the form is sent.

The snippets in this guide are plain HTML and JavaScript; adapt them to the project's framework and its version.

<!-- The first option's empty value is what makes required work: a placeholder      without value="" counts as a choice. --> <label for="country">Country</label> <select id="country" name="country" autocomplete="country" required>   <option value="">Choose a country</option>   <optgroup label="Europe">     <option value="DE">Germany</option>     <option value="PL">Poland</option>   </optgroup>   <optgroup label="Asia">     <option value="JP">Japan</option>   </optgroup> </select>

The combobox

  • Label: a visible <label for> on the input. The list is labelled by the same label (aria-labelledby).
  • Input: role="combobox", aria-autocomplete="list", aria-expanded, aria-controls pointing to the list, and aria-activedescendant while an option is highlighted. autocomplete="off" keeps the browser's own suggestions from covering the list. The combobox role goes on the input; the popup is always the listbox.
  • List: role="listbox", with options that have role="option", unique ids, and aria-selected="true" on the chosen one.
  • Value: a hidden input with the field's name holds the chosen option's value, so the form sends the choice, not the typed text. Hidden inputs are left out of constraint validation (checked), so required sits on the visible input, and any text there that isn't a choice, even only spaces, fails with a message such as "Choose a city from the list". A hidden input also can't restore its own value on a form reset, so the snippet keeps the page's starting choice and brings it back, with its text and aria-selected, after a reset. It waits for the reset event to finish and checks defaultPrevented first, since a later listener can cancel the reset, which keeps the current choice. It sets everything up the same way when the page loads.
  • Status region: one, present before it changes, for the number of results once typing pauses, "No matches", and loading.

Focus stays in the input the whole time, and nothing is trapped:

  • Typing filters the list and opens it, with nothing highlighted yet.
  • Down Arrow and Up Arrow open the list and move the highlight, wrapping at the ends. aria-activedescendant on the input points to the highlighted option, which scrolls into view.
  • Enter picks the highlighted option and closes the list. With nothing highlighted, it picks nothing. While the list is open, Enter never submits the form.
  • Space, Home, End, and letters type and move the caret, as in any text box, so "New York" can be typed.
  • While an input method editor (IME) composes text, such as Japanese, Chinese, or Korean, its keys are its own: the arrows, Enter, and Escape aren't handled. Check isComposing, and keyCode 229, which is how Safari reports the Enter that confirms a composition.
  • Escape closes the list and keeps the text. It doesn't close a dialog around the combobox: the snippet cancels the key while the list is open (checked in Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit). With the list closed, Escape does what it does around it.
  • Tab closes the list and moves on. Typed text isn't a choice unless an option was picked.
  • A click or tap on an option picks it, and focus stays in the input: cancel mousedown on the list. Cancelling pointerdown instead also stops a tap's click in WebKit (checked).
  • A click elsewhere closes the list, and focus stays where the click put it.
<label for="city" id="city-label">City</label> <div class="combobox">   <input id="city" type="text" role="combobox" autocomplete="off" required     aria-autocomplete="list" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="city-options">   <ul id="city-options" role="listbox" aria-labelledby="city-label" hidden>     <li id="city-krakow" role="option" aria-selected="false" data-value="krakow">Kraków</li>     <li id="city-new-york" role="option" aria-selected="false" data-value="new-york">New York</li>     <li id="city-newcastle" role="option" aria-selected="false" data-value="newcastle">Newcastle</li>   </ul>   <input type="hidden" name="city" id="city-value"> </div> 
// A searchable select, after the APG editable combobox. Focus stays in the input, and // aria-activedescendant points to the highlighted option. Space types, Enter picks only a // highlighted option, and the hidden input holds the choice that the form sends. const input = document.getElementById('city'); const list = document.getElementById('city-options'); const chosen = document.getElementById('city-value'); const options = [...list.querySelectorAll('[role="option"]')]; const visible = () => options.filter((option) => !option.hidden); const initial = chosen.value; // a hidden input can't restore its value on a form reset let active = -1; // the highlighted option's index among the visible ones  function highlight(index) {   active = index;   visible().forEach((option, i) => option.classList.toggle('is-highlighted', i === index));   const option = visible()[index];   if (option) input.setAttribute('aria-activedescendant', option.id);   else input.removeAttribute('aria-activedescendant');   option?.scrollIntoView({ block: 'nearest' }); }  function setOpen(open) {   list.hidden = !open;   input.setAttribute('aria-expanded', String(open));   highlight(-1); }  // Sets the choice, or none: the option's text in the input, its value in the hidden input, // and aria-selected on it alone. Text that isn't a choice, even only spaces, fails // validation; required on the input covers an empty one. function setChoice(option) {   for (const each of options) each.setAttribute('aria-selected', String(each === option));   chosen.value = option ? option.dataset.value : '';   if (option) input.value = option.textContent;   input.setCustomValidity(input.value !== '' && !option ? 'Choose a city from the list' : ''); }  function choose(option) {   setChoice(option);   setOpen(false); }  input.addEventListener('input', () => {   const query = input.value.trim().toLocaleLowerCase();   for (const option of options) option.hidden = !option.textContent.toLocaleLowerCase().includes(query);   setChoice(null); // typed text isn't a choice until an option is picked   setOpen(true); });  input.addEventListener('keydown', (event) => {   // While an input method composes text, these keys are its own; Safari reports the Enter   // that confirms a composition as keyCode 229   if (event.isComposing || event.keyCode === 229) return;   const count = visible().length;   if ((event.key === 'ArrowDown' || event.key === 'ArrowUp') && count > 0) {     event.preventDefault();     if (list.hidden) setOpen(true);     const down = event.key === 'ArrowDown';     if (active < 0) highlight(down ? 0 : count - 1);     else highlight((active + (down ? 1 : count - 1)) % count); // wraps around   } else if (event.key === 'Enter' && !list.hidden) {     event.preventDefault(); // while the list is open, Enter never submits the form     if (active >= 0) choose(visible()[active]); // with nothing highlighted, nothing is picked   } else if (event.key === 'Escape' && !list.hidden) {     event.preventDefault(); // closes only the list, not a dialog around it     setOpen(false);   } });  // Cancelling mousedown keeps focus in the input; a cancelled pointerdown would also stop // a tap's click in WebKit list.addEventListener('mousedown', (event) => event.preventDefault()); list.addEventListener('click', (event) => {   const option = event.target.closest('[role="option"]');   if (option) choose(option); }); input.addEventListener('blur', () => setOpen(false));  // The page's starting choice, set up now and again after a reset that wasn't cancelled: the // form puts the input's text back only after its reset event, and a listener after this one // can still cancel the reset function restore() {   for (const option of options) option.hidden = false;   choose(options.find((option) => option.dataset.value === initial) ?? null); } input.form?.addEventListener('reset', (event) => setTimeout(() => {   if (!event.defaultPrevented) restore(); })); restore();

Results from the server

  • Ask once typing pauses (about 300 ms, suggested), and say "Loading…" in the status region.
  • Answers can arrive out of order, so keep only the latest request's answer: number each request and ignore any other answer, or abort the previous request with an AbortController.
  • "No matches" and errors are text in the popup, not options, and are said in the status region.

Several choices

  • The list gets aria-multiselectable="true". Picking an option toggles its aria-selected, and the list stays open.
  • The chosen values show outside the input as a list, each with a Remove button named after its value ("Remove Kraków"). Interactive elements can't sit inside the input or another button.
  • Each chosen value goes to the form in its own hidden input with the field's name.
  • Optional: Backspace in an empty input removes the last value; say so in the hint.

Groups

In the list, a group is an element with role="group", labelled by its heading with aria-labelledby. The heading isn't an option, and the arrows skip it.

Rich options without search

The APG select-only combobox has no text box, so its keys differ from the searchable one's. The list, the hidden input with the value, and the reset work the same way.

  • Markup: a focusable element (tabindex="0") with role="combobox", named by the visible label with aria-labelledby, with aria-controls, aria-expanded, and aria-activedescendant while the list is open. Its text is the chosen option's text. It isn't a form field, so the form's own validation checks a required choice, and aria-required="true" says it.
  • Closed: Enter, Space, Down Arrow, and Alt+Down Arrow open the list without changing the choice. Up Arrow and Home open it on the first option, and End on the last. Typing letters opens it on the first option that starts with them.
  • Open: Down Arrow and Up Arrow move the highlight, stopping at the ends. Home and End go to the first and last option, and Page Up and Page Down jump 10 options. Enter, Space, and Alt+Up Arrow pick the highlighted option and close the list. Tab picks it, closes the list, and moves on. Escape closes the list without changing the choice. Typing letters moves to the first option that starts with them, and typing the same letter again moves through the options that start with it.
  • Focus stays on the combobox, and aria-activedescendant marks the highlighted option, as in the searchable one.

Appearance

These are suggested defaults; the project's design and tokens win.

  • The highlighted option is the focus indicator, since focus stays in the input. Give it at least 3:1 contrast against what's around it, with an outline or a solid background; a faint tint such as #eff6ff on white is 1.1:1. Style it with a class or a data attribute, not :focus: options never get focus.
  • Chosen options show a check, not color alone.
  • The list opens in the top layer (the popover attribute) or a portal, so a parent with overflow: hidden can't clip it. It sits below the input, or above it when there's no room, with CSS anchor positioning where the project's browsers support it, or the positioning code the project already has.
  • Sizes: a 44 px tall input, options at least 40 px tall (44 px on touch), 16 px text, and a list at most about 300 px tall that scrolls inside.
  • Motion is optional: the list fades in over 150 ms. Under prefers-reduced-motion: reduce, it appears without movement.

Edge cases

  • Many options: with hundreds, filter on the server or render only part of the list. Then each option needs aria-setsize and aria-posinset, since browsers can only count rendered options; otherwise leave them out.
  • Options that can't be chosen right now have aria-disabled="true", and the arrows still reach them, so screen reader users learn they exist; Enter and a click don't pick them (APG).
  • Edit forms start with the chosen option's text in the input and its value in the hidden input. The snippet sets aria-selected and the validity from them when the page loads, and brings them back after a form reset that wasn't cancelled.
  • In a dialog: the first Escape closes the list, and the second the dialog.
  • Before the script runs: a server-rendered page can start with the native select and replace it with the combobox once the script runs.

Acceptance checklist

  • [ ] A single choice without search uses the native select, and a required one starts with a placeholder option whose value is empty
  • [ ] The combobox and its list are named by the field's visible label
  • [ ] Typing filters the list without highlighting anything, and Space types a space
  • [ ] The arrow keys move the highlight with aria-activedescendant while focus stays in the input, and the highlight has at least 3:1 contrast
  • [ ] Enter picks only a highlighted option, and never submits the form while the list is open
  • [ ] Escape closes only the list, so a dialog around it stays open
  • [ ] A click or tap on an option picks it and keeps focus in the input, and a click elsewhere closes the list and leaves focus where the click was
  • [ ] The form sends the chosen value, not the typed text, and text that isn't a choice, even only spaces, fails validation with a message
  • [ ] A form reset brings back the starting choice, with its text and its selection, and a cancelled reset keeps the current one
  • [ ] While an input method composes text, the arrows, Enter, and Escape are left to it
  • [ ] A select-only combobox opens with Enter, Space, or the arrows, picks with Enter or Space, and finds options by the letters typed
  • [ ] With several choices, the list stays open, the chosen values show outside the input, and each Remove button names its value
  • [ ] Results, "No matches", and loading are announced through one status region, and an older search answer never replaces a newer one
  • [ ] The list isn't clipped by its container, and works on a phone and at 320 px wide
  • [ ] Styles come from the project's styling system and tokens, like its other form controls

See also

  • Text Input Field: the same label, hint, and error wiring.
  • Form Validation Pattern: when errors appear, and where focus goes when a form is submitted.
  • Login & Registration Forms: registration forms that ask for a country or a language.

These are suggestions; the select works in any form.
excerpt: Choosing from a list: the native select for a simple choice, and a combobox for search and several choices that keeps focus in its input, highlights with aria-activedescendant, and never picks or submits anything by accident.

title: Modal Dialog
body:
A modal dialog stops the page for a decision or a short task, then returns people to where they were. This guide builds on the dialog your project already has, or on the browser's native <dialog>, and targets WCAG 2.2 AA.

When to use something else

  • Information that needs no answer: show it in the page, or as a toast.
  • A long or multi-step task: give it its own page.
  • A short list of choices: use a menu or a popover.

Start from what the project has

  1. If the project has a dialog or modal component, in its design system or a library it already uses, configure or extend it to meet this guide. Keep its API.
  2. Otherwise use native <dialog> and open it with showModal(). The browser draws it in the top layer with its own backdrop (::backdrop), and makes the rest of the page inert, so nothing behind it can be clicked or focused. Don't show a modal with the open attribute or show(): they give a non-modal dialog without a backdrop or an inert page.
  3. Only if neither fits, build one from a container element (see "Without native dialog").

Implement only the options the task needs, and add no dependency, such as a focus-trap or scroll-lock library, without asking. The project's conventions win for styling and visual defaults. If one conflicts with an accessibility or correctness requirement here, ask instead of choosing.

Structure

  • Trigger: the control that opens the dialog.
  • Title: a visible heading that names the dialog (aria-labelledby).
  • Description (optional): one short plain-text message, as in a confirmation (aria-describedby). Leave it out when the body holds a form or longer content, which a screen reader would read in full on open.
  • Body: the content. It scrolls inside the dialog when it's long.
  • Status message: an element with role="status", present from the moment the dialog opens, for busy and error text.
  • Actions: Cancel and the primary action, named for what it does ("Delete project", not "OK").
  • Close button (optional): an icon button with an accessible name such as "Close".

Every dialog has a visible Cancel or Close button, because touch and screen reader users may have no Escape key. Use role="alertdialog" for an urgent decision, such as confirming a deletion. Native <dialog> is already a dialog; add aria-modal="true" only to a dialog that isn't native. On the trigger, aria-haspopup="dialog" is optional (never "true", which announces a menu), and aria-expanded is rarely useful for a modal.

Opening and focus

When the dialog opens, focus moves to:

  • the least destructive action, usually Cancel, in confirmations and alert dialogs
  • the first field in a form
  • the title or the top of the content (tabindex="-1") when the content is long or should be read first
  • otherwise the first focusable element

With native <dialog>, put autofocus on that element. While the dialog is open, Tab and Shift+Tab move through its controls and never reach the page behind it. (With native <dialog>, they can also reach the browser's own controls.) Every control shows a visible focus indicator with at least 3:1 contrast.

Closing

  • Escape closes a dismissible dialog that isn't busy. Escape, and the back gesture on Android, sends a close request: native <dialog> fires cancel, then close. To keep a dialog open that isn't dismissible, call preventDefault() on cancel. Browsers may still close it on a repeated request without other user interaction, so treat every close as the safe choice, Cancel, never as a confirmation.
  • Cancel and Close always close it, except while the primary action runs (see below).
  • A backdrop click closes a dismissible dialog when closeOnBackdropClick is on, and only when the press also started on the backdrop. A text selection dragged from inside the dialog onto the backdrop ends in a click on the dialog, and must not close it. Give the native <dialog> no padding of its own, so only a backdrop click targets it. Where the browser supports it, closedby="any" does this natively; keep the script for the others. Turn backdrop closing off for alert dialogs, and for forms with typed input.

After every close, focus returns to the trigger; native <dialog> does this itself. If the trigger is gone, for example because Delete removed its row, move focus to a sensible place nearby: the next item, the list, or its heading with tabindex="-1". Never leave focus on the page body. If the list updates only after the dialog has closed, move focus when it updates.

The primary action

  • While it runs, the dialog stays open, and the status message says what's happening ("Deleting…"). The actions get aria-disabled="true" and ignore activation. Don't use the disabled attribute, which drops focus from the button to the page.
  • On success, the dialog closes.
  • On failure, it stays open, the status message shows the error, and the actions work again with focus still on the primary action, so the person can retry or cancel.
  • Give the request a time limit, for example 30 seconds (AbortSignal.timeout() with fetch). When it runs out, show an error that says so, and make the actions work again, so the person can retry or cancel. Tell a timeout from other failures by the signal's reason (signal.reason.name is "TimeoutError"), not by the error: WebKit rejects fetch with an AbortError.
  • While it runs, Escape and backdrop clicks do nothing. Cancel and Close abort it only when aborting really stops the work, such as an upload or a search. A request that changes data can still finish on the server, so for that they wait.
  • If the browser closes the dialog anyway, for example after a repeated Escape or back gesture, show the result in the page, for example in a toast. If focus was lost with the trigger, move it as described under "Closing". Opened again before the result arrives, the dialog shows the busy state again.
  • In a form dialog, the primary action validates first. On errors the dialog stays open, and focus moves to the first invalid field. <form method="dialog"> closes the dialog on submit and sets returnValue, which is enough for confirmations without async work.

The page behind

  • Native <dialog> and inert stop clicks and focus behind the dialog, but not scrolling. Set overflow: hidden on the root element while a modal is open: html:has(dialog:modal).
  • Keep the scrollbar's space, so the layout doesn't jump: scrollbar-gutter: stable on the root, or padding equal to the scrollbar's width while the page is locked.
  • Give the dialog's scrolling body overscroll-behavior: contain, so scrolling it doesn't scroll the page at its ends.
  • iOS Safari can still scroll the page under a touch. Where it does, fix the body in place while the dialog is open (position: fixed, with top set to minus the scroll position), and restore the scroll position on close.

Layout

These are suggested defaults; the project's design and tokens win.

  • From 768 px wide: centered, at most 640 px wide and calc(100dvh - 64px) tall, with 24 px padding. The title row and the actions stay visible while the body scrolls.
  • Below 768 px: full screen when fullscreenOnMobile is on: 100vw wide (100% would leave a reserved scrollbar gutter uncovered), 100dvh tall, no margins or rounded corners, and padding that includes the safe-area insets. Otherwise near-full width with 16 px gutters. dvh keeps the dialog clear of the browser's toolbars; keep 100vh as the fallback.
  • Short viewports (under about 480 px tall: landscape phones, high zoom): the whole content scrolls, actions included.
  • 320 px wide (400% zoom on a 1280 px screen): nothing scrolls sideways.
  • A scrolling body that holds no focusable element is focusable itself (tabindex="0") and named, so keyboard users can scroll it.
  • The close button and the actions are at least 24 by 24 px; 40 px is a comfortable size for the close button.
  • The browser stylesheet gives dialog:modal default margins and maximum sizes; override them for the full-screen layout.

Motion

Motion is optional. Open in 180 ms and close in 140 ms with cubic-bezier(0.2, 0, 0, 1): the backdrop fades, and the dialog fades in from translateY(8px) scale(0.98). For native <dialog>, animate the open with @starting-style. Animating the close also needs transition-behavior: allow-discrete on display and overlay; where a browser can't do that, the dialog closes at once, which is fine. Focus returns and the page unlocks at once, not after the animation. Under prefers-reduced-motion: reduce, nothing moves: a short fade, or no animation.

Example

A delete confirmation in plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. Adapt it to the project's framework, its version, and its styling system. deleteProject() and notify() stand for the app's own request and its toast or page message.

<button type="button" id="delete-trigger">Delete project</button>  <dialog id="confirm-delete" role="alertdialog" aria-labelledby="confirm-title" aria-describedby="confirm-message">   <div class="dialog-inner">     <h2 id="confirm-title">Delete project?</h2>     <div class="dialog-body">       <p id="confirm-message">This deletes the project and its files for everyone on the team.</p>     </div>     <p class="dialog-status" role="status"></p>     <div class="dialog-actions">       <button type="button" data-action="cancel" autofocus>Cancel</button>       <button type="button" data-action="confirm">Delete project</button>     </div>   </div> </dialog> 
dialog {   padding: 0; /* .dialog-inner has the padding, so only the backdrop targets <dialog> itself */   border: none;   border-radius: 12px;   width: min(640px, 100% - 32px);   max-height: calc(100dvh - 64px); }  dialog::backdrop {   background: rgb(0 0 0 / 0.5); }  .dialog-inner {   display: flex;   flex-direction: column;   gap: 16px;   box-sizing: border-box;   max-height: inherit;   padding: 24px; }  .dialog-body {   overflow: auto;   overscroll-behavior: contain; }  .dialog-actions {   display: flex;   flex-wrap: wrap;   justify-content: flex-end;   gap: 12px; }  .dialog-actions [aria-disabled='true'] {   cursor: not-allowed;   opacity: 0.6; }  /* The page doesn't scroll behind a modal, and keeps the scrollbar's space so nothing shifts */ html {   scrollbar-gutter: stable; }  html:has(dialog:modal) {   overflow: hidden; }  /* Short viewports (landscape phones, high zoom): everything scrolls, the actions included */ @media (max-height: 480px) {   .dialog-inner {     overflow: auto;     overscroll-behavior: contain;   }    .dialog-body {     overflow: visible;   } }  /* Phones: full screen, clear of the browser's toolbars and the screen's rounded corners */ @media (max-width: 767px) {   dialog.fullscreen-mobile {     width: 100vw; /* 100% would leave the reserved scrollbar gutter uncovered */     max-width: none;     height: 100vh;     height: 100dvh;     max-height: none;     margin: 0;     border-radius: 0;   }    dialog.fullscreen-mobile .dialog-inner {     height: 100%;     padding: max(16px, env(safe-area-inset-top)) max(16px, env(safe-area-inset-right))       max(16px, env(safe-area-inset-bottom)) max(16px, env(safe-area-inset-left));   } } 
// Opens a modal <dialog> with this guide's closing and focus rules. // fallbackFocus: where focus goes if the trigger is gone when the dialog closes. function openDialog(dialog, trigger, { dismissible = true, closeOnBackdropClick = true, fallbackFocus } = {}) {   let pressStartedOnBackdrop = false;    // <dialog> has no padding, so only the backdrop makes it the event target. A text selection   // dragged from inside also ends in a click on <dialog>, so the press must start there too.   const onPointerDown = (event) => {     pressStartedOnBackdrop = event.target === dialog;   };   const onClick = (event) => {     const fromBackdrop = pressStartedOnBackdrop && event.target === dialog;     pressStartedOnBackdrop = false;     if (fromBackdrop && dismissible && closeOnBackdropClick && dialog.dataset.busy !== 'true') {       dialog.close('cancel');     }   };   // Escape, or the back gesture on Android. A repeated request may still close the dialog, so   // a close without returnValue 'confirm' always counts as Cancel.   const onCancel = (event) => {     if (!dismissible || dialog.dataset.busy === 'true') event.preventDefault();   };   const onClose = () => {     dialog.removeEventListener('pointerdown', onPointerDown);     dialog.removeEventListener('click', onClick);     dialog.removeEventListener('cancel', onCancel);     (trigger.isConnected ? trigger : fallbackFocus)?.focus();   };    dialog.returnValue = '';   dialog.addEventListener('pointerdown', onPointerDown);   dialog.addEventListener('click', onClick);   dialog.addEventListener('cancel', onCancel);   dialog.addEventListener('close', onClose, { once: true });   dialog.showModal(); }  // The delete confirmation: an alert dialog that a backdrop click doesn't close. // deleteProject() and notify() stand for the app's request and its toast or page message. const trigger = document.getElementById('delete-trigger'); const dialog = document.getElementById('confirm-delete'); const status = dialog.querySelector('[role="status"]'); const actions = dialog.querySelectorAll('.dialog-actions button'); const heading = document.getElementById('projects-heading'); // the list's heading, tabindex="-1"  trigger.addEventListener('click', () => {   // Opened again while the request still runs: keep its busy message   if (dialog.dataset.busy !== 'true') status.textContent = '';   openDialog(dialog, trigger, { closeOnBackdropClick: false, fallbackFocus: heading }); });  dialog.querySelector('[data-action="cancel"]').addEventListener('click', () => {   if (dialog.dataset.busy !== 'true') dialog.close('cancel'); });  // The browser can close the dialog while the request runs (a repeated Escape or back gesture), // so a result that arrives after that goes to the page, and lost focus goes to the heading function report(message) {   if (dialog.open) {     status.textContent = message;     return;   }   notify(message);   if (!trigger.isConnected && document.activeElement === document.body) heading.focus(); }  dialog.querySelector('[data-action="confirm"]').addEventListener('click', async () => {   if (dialog.dataset.busy === 'true') return;   // Busy: the buttons keep focus (aria-disabled, not disabled), and the status message says why   dialog.dataset.busy = 'true';   actions.forEach((button) => button.setAttribute('aria-disabled', 'true'));   status.textContent = 'Deleting…';   // A time limit, so a request that hangs can't trap anyone   const signal = AbortSignal.timeout(30_000);   try {     await deleteProject({ signal }); // on success it also removes the project's row, trigger included     if (dialog.open) dialog.close('confirm');     else report('Project deleted.');   } catch {     // Ask the signal, not the error: WebKit rejects fetch with an AbortError, not the TimeoutError     report(signal.reason?.name === 'TimeoutError'       ? 'Deleting is taking too long. Check your connection and try again.'       : "The project wasn't deleted. Check your connection and try again.");   } finally {     dialog.dataset.busy = 'false';     actions.forEach((button) => button.removeAttribute('aria-disabled'));   } });

Without native dialog

Only when neither the project nor native <dialog> fits, for example an overlay system the project must keep:

  • Render the dialog at the end of body with role="dialog" (or "alertdialog") and aria-modal="true".
  • Make every sibling of its container inert while it's open. That keeps focus in the dialog, so no focus-trap library is needed. Don't hide the page with aria-hidden instead.
  • Move focus in and return it as above, and close on Escape with a keydown listener on the dialog.
  • Give the backdrop element the same press-and-click check.
  • Put the backdrop and the dialog at the top of the project's layering scale, above sticky bars, dropdowns, popovers, and toasts.

Edge cases

  • Stacked dialogs: avoid a dialog on top of a dialog; replace the content instead. When it can't be avoided, showModal() stacks it: Escape closes the top one, and focus returns into the one below. Without native <dialog>, make the lower dialog inert too.
  • Toasts: a toast below an open modal can't be reached. Show the result of the dialog's action after it closes, or inside the dialog while it stays open.
  • Double clicks: ignore the trigger while the dialog opens or closes, so a double click never opens two.
  • Navigation: if the route changes while the dialog is open, close it without returning focus to a trigger on the old page.
  • Server rendering: render the dialog closed, and call showModal() only in the browser, after mount.
  • Unsaved input (optional): a form dialog can ask before discarding typed input.

Acceptance checklist

  • [ ] Opened from the keyboard, focus lands as the initial-focus rule says, and a screen reader announces the dialog's role and title, plus its short description if it has one
  • [ ] Tab and Shift+Tab never reach the page behind it, and the page can't be clicked or scrolled, including by touch on iOS Safari
  • [ ] Opening it doesn't shift the page's layout
  • [ ] Escape closes a dismissible dialog, and focus returns to the trigger; a dialog that isn't dismissible stays open on the first Escape, and any close counts as Cancel
  • [ ] A backdrop click closes the dialog only when that's turned on, and dragging a text selection from inside onto the backdrop never closes it
  • [ ] Every dialog has a visible Cancel or Close button with an accessible name, at least 24 by 24 px
  • [ ] While the primary action runs, focus stays on its button and the status message announces progress; a failure keeps the dialog open with the error announced and the buttons working; a success closes it
  • [ ] A request that never settles ends at its time limit with an error and working buttons, and a result that arrives after the dialog closed shows in the page without leaving focus on the page body
  • [ ] When the action removed the trigger, focus lands in a sensible place nearby, not on the page body
  • [ ] At 320 px wide and at 400% zoom nothing scrolls sideways and the actions stay reachable; on phones, the full-screen dialog isn't hidden behind the browser's toolbars
  • [ ] With reduced motion, nothing moves
  • [ ] Styles come from the project's styling system and tokens, like its other components

See also

  • Button: for the dialog's actions.
  • Toast Notifications: toasts sit below an open modal, so show an action's result after the dialog closes.

These are suggestions; the dialog works with any button or notification implementation.
excerpt: An accessible modal dialog for confirmations and short tasks, built on the project's dialog component or the native dialog element: focus that moves in and comes back, Escape and backdrop rules, a busy state that survives a failed action, and a full-screen layout on phones.

title: Data Table (Sortable, Paginated, Filterable)
body:
A data table is where people find and act on records. Its problems are mostly about reach and state: header cells that only a mouse can sort, aria-sort on every column, focusable rows that add a Tab stop each, a header checkbox that counts rows on other pages, and a Next button that drops focus on the last page. This guide covers a plain, sortable, filterable, paginated table with selection, and targets WCAG 2.2 AA.

Start from what the project has

  1. If the project has a data table, or a table library it already uses, configure or extend it to meet this guide. Keep its API.
  2. Otherwise build it from a plain <table>.

Implement only what the task needs, and add no dependency without asking. The project's conventions win for styling and visual defaults. If one conflicts with an accessibility or correctness requirement here, ask instead of choosing.

Structure

  • It's a real <table>. A <caption> names it, or aria-labelledby points to its heading. Column headers are <th scope="col">, and the cell that identifies a row, such as a name, is a <th scope="row">, so screen readers say whose row a cell is in.
  • It's a plain table, not a grid: Tab moves between its controls (sort buttons, checkboxes, links), and rows and cells aren't focusable. Arrow-key navigation between cells belongs to the grid pattern (role="grid", one Tab stop, editing keys), which this guide doesn't cover.
  • Numbers are right-aligned, with tabular figures, and dates are <time datetime> elements.
  • A table wider than its container scrolls inside a region with role="region", named by the caption, and tabindex="0", so keyboard users can scroll to columns that have nothing focusable.
  • A cell that's cut short still gives a way to the whole value: let it wrap, or show it in the row's details.

Sorting

  • A sortable column has a <button> inside its <th>, named by the column's name; the header cell itself can't take focus. As in the APG sortable table example, the caption says that the column buttons sort.
  • aria-sort ("ascending" or "descending") is only on the sorted column's <th>. The other headers have none; ARIA allows one sorted header at a time.
  • A click on the sorted column reverses it, and a click on another column sorts it ascending. A third state that restores the original order is optional.
  • Each column compares by its type: numbers as numbers, dates by their value, and text with Intl.Collator (numeric: true), so "Émile" sorts with E, and "Item 2" comes before "Item 10".
  • The status region says how the table is sorted ("Sorted by Name, ascending"), and sorting goes back to page 1.
  • With sorting on the server, send the column and the direction, set aria-sort when the answer arrives, and let only the latest answer fill the table.

The snippets in this guide are plain HTML and JavaScript; adapt them to the project's framework and its version. The two scripts share the table; status is the table's status region, and pageShown() runs after a page of rows is rendered.

<p class="table-status visually-hidden" role="status"></p> <p class="selection-count"></p> <!-- The region scrolls sideways when the table is wider than the page; tabindex lets the      keyboard scroll it --> <div class="table-scroll" role="region" aria-labelledby="customers-caption" tabindex="0">   <table class="customers">     <caption id="customers-caption">Customers <span class="visually-hidden">(the column buttons sort the table)</span></caption>     <thead>       <tr>         <th scope="col"><input type="checkbox" class="select-all" aria-label="Select all customers on this page"></th>         <th scope="col" aria-sort="ascending"><button type="button">Name</button></th>         <th scope="col" data-type="number"><button type="button">Orders</button></th>         <th scope="col" data-type="date"><button type="button">Last order</button></th>       </tr>     </thead>     <tbody>       <tr>         <td><input type="checkbox" value="c-1042" aria-label="Select Émile Zola"></td>         <th scope="row">Émile Zola</th>         <td>12</td>         <td data-value="2026-10-02"><time datetime="2026-10-02">2 Oct 2026</time></td>       </tr>       <!-- one row per customer on this page -->     </tbody>   </table> </div> 
// Sortable headers, after the APG sortable table: a button in each sortable <th>, aria-sort on // the sorted column only, and a comparison for each column's type. Text sorts with // Intl.Collator, so "Émile" sorts with E, and "Item 2" comes before "Item 10". const table = document.querySelector('.customers'); const status = document.querySelector('.table-status'); const collator = new Intl.Collator(undefined, { numeric: true, sensitivity: 'base' }); const compare = {   text: (a, b) => collator.compare(a, b),   number: (a, b) => Number(a) - Number(b),   date: (a, b) => (a < b ? -1 : a > b ? 1 : 0), // ISO dates in data-value sort as text };  table.tHead.addEventListener('click', (event) => {   const button = event.target.closest('th button');   if (!button) return;   const header = button.closest('th');   const direction = header.getAttribute('aria-sort') === 'ascending' ? 'descending' : 'ascending';   for (const th of table.tHead.querySelectorAll('th')) th.removeAttribute('aria-sort');   header.setAttribute('aria-sort', direction);   const value = (row) => row.cells[header.cellIndex].dataset.value ?? row.cells[header.cellIndex].textContent.trim();   const sign = direction === 'ascending' ? 1 : -1;   const rows = [...table.tBodies[0].rows].sort((a, b) => sign * compare[header.dataset.type ?? 'text'](value(a), value(b)));   table.tBodies[0].append(...rows);   status.textContent = `Sorted by ${button.textContent}, ${direction}`; });

Filtering

  • One labelled filter field above the table ("Filter customers", an <input type="search">) narrows the rows by their text, in the browser or on the server.
  • Once typing pauses, the status region says how many rows match ("12 customers"). With none, the table says "No customers match", with a Clear filter button.
  • A new filter goes back to page 1, and only the latest answer counts: number the requests, or abort the previous one.
  • Rows the filter hides stay selected, and the selection toolbar counts them with the rows on other pages.
  • Optional: filters for single columns, such as a status select, in the same bar above the table, each with a visible label, and a Clear all button. The filter's value can also go in the URL, so a link opens the same view.

Pages

  • Below the table: Previous and Next, page numbers from 768 px, a "Rows per page" select (10, 25, 50, or 100), and a summary ("Showing 11–20 of 245").
  • Previous on the first page and Next on the last use aria-disabled="true" and ignore presses. The native disabled attribute on a focused Next, as the last page loads, drops focus to the page (checked in Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit).
  • The current page's button has aria-current="page", and page buttons are named with the word ("Page 3"), visible or visually hidden.
  • The status region says the new summary after a page change. If the page scrolls to the table's top, focus moves there too, to the caption or the table's heading (tabindex="-1"); otherwise the scroll position stays.
  • A new page size goes back to page 1. The page and its size can go in the URL. With pages on the server, send the page and the size, and show the total the server returns.

Selection

  • Each row has a checkbox named after the row ("Select Émile Zola"), and the header has one for the page ("Select all customers on this page"). The checkbox is the one control: rows get neither tabindex nor aria-selected, which belong to the grid pattern.
  • The selection is kept by row id across pages and the filter. The header checkbox shows only this page: checked when every row on it is selected, and partly checked (indeterminate, read as "mixed") when some are.
  • Optional: Shift and a click selects the rows between the last one clicked and this one. Keyboard users check rows one at a time.
  • The selection toolbar's space is reserved above the table, so rows don't move under the pointer when it appears. It says how many rows are selected and how many of them aren't on this page ("5 selected, 2 not on this page"), with Clear selection and the bulk actions, named with the count ("Delete 5 customers"). Delete asks first or offers undo, as the Modal Dialog guide describes.
  • Optional: after the page is selected, the toolbar offers "Select all 245 customers".
// Row checkboxes, and the header checkbox for this page. The selection is kept by row id // across pages and filters; the header checkbox shows only this page: checked when every row // on it is selected, partly checked (indeterminate) when some are. const selectAll = table.querySelector('.select-all'); const count = document.querySelector('.selection-count'); const selected = new Set(); const boxes = () => [...table.tBodies[0].querySelectorAll('input[type="checkbox"]')];  function update() {   const onPage = boxes().filter((box) => box.checked).length;   selectAll.checked = onPage > 0 && onPage === boxes().length;   selectAll.indeterminate = onPage > 0 && onPage < boxes().length;   const elsewhere = selected.size - onPage;   count.textContent = selected.size === 0 ? '' : `${selected.size} selected${elsewhere ? `, ${elsewhere} not on this page` : ''}`; } function setRow(box, checked) {   box.checked = checked;   if (checked) selected.add(box.value);   else selected.delete(box.value); } table.tBodies[0].addEventListener('change', (event) => {   if (event.target.type === 'checkbox') setRow(event.target, event.target.checked);   update(); }); selectAll.addEventListener('change', () => {   for (const box of boxes()) setRow(box, selectAll.checked);   update(); }); // After a page of rows is rendered (paging, sorting on the server, filtering) function pageShown() {   for (const box of boxes()) box.checked = selected.has(box.value);   update(); }

Loading, empty, and error

  • While loading, skeleton rows keep the table's shape and are hidden from screen readers (aria-hidden="true"); the status region says "Loading customers…". The header stays.
  • Empty, the table says why, with the next step: "No customers yet" with the action that adds one, or, with a filter, "No customers match" with Clear filter.
  • On an error, the table shows a message and Retry, in text. Server errors and stack traces stay in the logs.
  • Each table keeps its own loading, empty, and error states, so it still works on its own.

Phones

  • Below 768 px, rows can become cards in a list (<ul>), each card's fields a description list (<dl>), with the row's name as the card's heading. The checkboxes stay, named after their rows; sorting moves to a "Sort by" select, and pagination to Previous and Next.
  • When the columns need to be compared side by side, keep the table, scrolling in its region, instead.

Sticky header

Optional: a sticky header row. Inside the horizontal scroll region, it doesn't stick to the page, since the region is its scroll container (checked in Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit). Use one per table: a sticky header without sideways scrolling, with top at the height of any sticky bar above it, or a region with a maximum height that scrolls both ways.

Variations

  • Row details: a disclosure button in the row ("Show details for Émile Zola") with aria-expanded, and the details in the next row, across all columns.
  • Editing in cells is the grid pattern, beyond this guide; editing in a form or a dialog keeps the table plain.
  • Reordering rows or columns, or resizing columns, by dragging needs a way without dragging (WCAG 2.2 2.5.7), such as Move up and Move down buttons, or a width setting.

Appearance

These are suggested defaults; the project's design and tokens win.

  • Rows are 48 to 52 px tall, with 12 to 16 px of padding in each cell.
  • Text meets 4.5:1; sort icons, checkbox edges, and focus indicators 3:1. The current page's button can be #2563eb with white text (5.2:1); #3b82f6 is only 3.7:1. Muted text can be #6b7280 (4.8:1 on white); #9ca3af is 2.5:1. Check the project's own colors.
  • A selected row is marked by its checkbox and a background, not by color alone.

Edge cases

  • One page: the pagination can go; the summary stays.
  • Many columns: the table scrolls in its region, or less important columns hide on smaller screens, never the row header.
  • Thousands of rows: use pages, or render only part of the rows; then the table gets aria-rowcount and each row aria-rowindex.
  • Sorting a selection: rows move with their checkboxes, and the selection stays.
  • Deleting rows: afterwards, focus moves somewhere sensible nearby, such as the caption or the next row's checkbox, never the page's body.

Acceptance checklist

  • [ ] It's a table with a caption, column headers with scope="col", and a row header for the cell that names each row
  • [ ] Sortable columns have a button inside the header, and aria-sort is on the sorted column only
  • [ ] Numbers sort as numbers, dates by their value, and text by language with Intl.Collator, and the status region says how the table is sorted
  • [ ] The filter field is labelled; a new filter goes back to page 1, only the latest answer counts, and the number of matches is said once typing pauses
  • [ ] Previous and Next at the ends use aria-disabled, so focus stays on them, and the current page has aria-current="page"
  • [ ] If a page change scrolls to the table, focus moves to the table too
  • [ ] Each row's checkbox is named after its row, and rows aren't focusable themselves
  • [ ] The header checkbox shows only this page: checked when all its rows are selected, mixed when some are
  • [ ] The selection is kept across pages and the filter, and the toolbar says how many selected rows aren't on this page
  • [ ] The toolbar's space is reserved, so rows don't move when it appears, and Delete asks first or offers undo
  • [ ] A wide table scrolls inside a named region with tabindex="0", and the page doesn't scroll sideways
  • [ ] Skeleton rows are hidden from screen readers, and empty and error states say what happened in text, with Clear filter or Retry
  • [ ] On phones, rows are cards in a list with their fields in a description list, or the table scrolls in its region
  • [ ] Styles come from the project's styling system and tokens

See also

  • Dashboard Layout with Collapsible Sidebar: the app shell around the table, whose main column wide tables can't widen.
  • Tabs Component: views of the table, such as All, Open, and Archived, in tab panels.
  • Modal Dialog: confirming a bulk delete.
  • Select and Combobox: filters for single columns.

These are suggestions; the table works on its own.
excerpt: A table for browsing records, with sortable headers, a filter field, and pages, and a selection kept across pages with a header checkbox for the page. It stays a real table, with a caption and row headers.

title: Command Palette
body:
A command palette is a search box for an app's destinations and actions, in a dialog that one shortcut opens. It is mostly a combobox, and its problems are a combobox's: an ARIA model left open, a highlight nobody can see, focus returned to a trigger that wasn't used, an Escape that only clears the text, and an older search's answer replacing a newer one. This guide follows the APG combobox with automatic selection and targets WCAG 2.2 AA.

Start from what the project has

  1. If the project has a command menu, or a combobox it can build on, in its design system or a library it already uses, configure or extend it to meet this guide. Keep its API.
  2. Otherwise build it from a native <dialog>, a text input, and a list.

Implement only what the task needs, and add no dependency without asking. The project's conventions win for styling and visual defaults. If one conflicts with an accessibility or correctness requirement here, ask instead of choosing.

Opening and closing

  • Cmd+K on macOS and Ctrl+K elsewhere open it. A visible trigger in the header ("Search" or "Commands") shows the shortcut for the person's system, ⌘K or Ctrl K, and has aria-keyshortcuts="Meta+K Control+K".
  • Don't take over Cmd or Ctrl+P, which is the browser's Print, or other browser shortcuts. When focus is in a rich text editor that uses the same shortcut, the editor keeps it.
  • The palette is a native <dialog> opened with showModal(), as in the Modal Dialog guide: focus goes into the search box, and the rest of the page is inert.
  • Escape closes it, with text in the box too. The input is type="text": in a type="search" field inside a modal dialog, Chromium and Firefox clear the text on the first Escape and keep the palette open, while WebKit closes it at once (checked).
  • Focus returns to the element that had focus before it opened, which the native dialog does by itself (checked in Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit). The shortcut usually opens it, so that isn't the trigger. After a command navigates, focus goes where the new page puts it.
  • A visible Close button is always there, since touch screens and many tablets have no Escape key; a button in a <form method="dialog"> closes the dialog without a script.

The search box and the results

  • The search box follows the APG combobox with list autocomplete and automatic selection. The input has role="combobox", aria-autocomplete="list", aria-expanded="true" (the list always shows), and aria-controls pointing to the list, and it's labelled "Search commands", visibly or visually hidden. autocomplete="off" and spellcheck="false" keep the browser's suggestions out of the way.
  • The results are a role="listbox" of role="option" rows with unique ids. Groups are role="group" elements, labelled by their headings.
  • Focus stays in the input. The highlighted command is the input's aria-activedescendant, with aria-selected="true", and scrolls into view.
  • The first result is highlighted whenever the list changes, so Enter runs it. Select and Combobox highlights nothing until an arrow key, because a picked option fills a form; a palette runs commands, and destructive ones ask first.
  • Down and Up Arrow move the highlight and wrap at the ends, through the options in the order on screen: build the order from the rendered list, not from the ranked array, since grouping reorders the ranks. Space types, and while an input method composes text, its keys are its own (isComposing, and keyCode 229 in Safari).
  • A click runs a command, and focus stays in the input: cancel mousedown on the list. The highlight follows the pointer only when the pointer really moves. Scrolling the list under a still pointer fires pointerover and mouseover in all three engines, and pointermove too in WebKit (checked), so a move counts only from a known, different position. An arrow key makes the position unknown again, since a mouse resting over the list may not have moved since the palette opened.
  • The highlight is the focus indicator, since focus stays in the input: give it 3:1 contrast against what's around it, with an outline or a solid background. A faint tint such as bg-neutral-100 on white is 1.1:1. Style it from aria-selected or a class, not :focus; options never get focus.
  • A command that's shown but can't run right now stays reachable with the arrows, has aria-disabled="true", and Enter doesn't run it (APG). Commands the person can never run are left out. Hiding them is only for convenience: the server checks permission when a command runs.

The snippets in this guide are plain HTML and JavaScript; adapt them to the project's framework and its version. runCommand() and findCommands() stand for the app's commands and its search; the two scripts share the input, the list, and highlight().

<dialog class="palette" aria-labelledby="palette-label">   <label class="visually-hidden" id="palette-label" for="palette-input">Search commands</label>   <!-- type="text": in a type="search" field, Escape clears the text in some browsers instead of closing -->   <input id="palette-input" type="text" role="combobox" autocomplete="off" spellcheck="false"     aria-autocomplete="list" aria-expanded="true" aria-controls="palette-results">   <form method="dialog"><button class="palette-close">Close</button></form>   <ul id="palette-results" role="listbox" aria-labelledby="palette-label"></ul>   <p class="palette-status visually-hidden" role="status"></p> </dialog> 
// The search box, after the APG combobox with automatic selection: focus stays in the input, // aria-activedescendant marks the highlighted command, and the first result is highlighted // whenever the list changes, so Enter runs it. Space types, and keys that belong to an input // method are left to it. Escape is the dialog's own: it closes the palette. const input = document.getElementById('palette-input'); const list = document.getElementById('palette-results'); // The results that can run, in the order on screen: none while a search is out (the list is busy) const options = () => (list.getAttribute('aria-busy') === 'true' ? [] : [...list.querySelectorAll('[role="option"]')]); let active = -1; let pointer = null; // the pointer's last position; unknown again after an arrow key  function highlight(index, scroll = true) {   active = index;   options().forEach((option, i) => option.setAttribute('aria-selected', String(i === index)));   const option = options()[index];   if (option) input.setAttribute('aria-activedescendant', option.id);   else input.removeAttribute('aria-activedescendant');   if (option && scroll) option.scrollIntoView({ block: 'nearest' }); } function run(option) {   if (options().includes(option) && option.getAttribute('aria-disabled') !== 'true') runCommand(option.dataset.command); } input.addEventListener('keydown', (event) => {   const count = options().length;   if (event.isComposing || event.keyCode === 229 || count === 0) return;   if (event.key === 'ArrowDown' || event.key === 'ArrowUp') {     event.preventDefault();     pointer = null;     highlight((active + (event.key === 'ArrowDown' ? 1 : -1) + count) % count);   } else if (event.key === 'Enter' && active >= 0) {     event.preventDefault();     run(options()[active]);   } }); list.addEventListener('mousedown', (event) => event.preventDefault()); // focus stays in the input list.addEventListener('click', (event) => run(event.target.closest('[role="option"]'))); // The highlight follows the pointer only when it moves. Scrolling the list under a still // pointer fires pointermove in WebKit, so a move counts only from a known, different position. list.addEventListener('pointermove', (event) => {   const position = `${event.clientX},${event.clientY}`;   const moved = pointer !== null && position !== pointer;   pointer = position;   const option = event.target.closest('[role="option"]');   if (moved && option) highlight(options().indexOf(option), false); });

Searching

  • Matching is up to the app: fuzzy matching, keywords and aliases, and ranking by prefix, recent use, and the current context. Matched characters show in bold, not only in color.
  • With an empty box, show recent and suggested commands. Recent commands are kept under the app's own storage prefix, as ids, never with their data.
  • Only the latest search's answer fills the list: number the requests and drop older answers, or abort the previous request.
  • While a search is out, the previous results stay in view but can't run: nothing is highlighted, the list has aria-busy="true" (which the project's styles can dim), Enter and clicks do nothing, and the previous announcement is cancelled. Otherwise, with results from a server, Enter in that moment runs a command from the previous query.
  • One status region, present from the start, says the number of results once typing pauses ("3 commands"), "No matching commands", and failures. It doesn't speak on every key.
  • A long list can render only part of itself; then the highlighted option stays rendered, and every option has aria-setsize and aria-posinset.
// Only the latest search's answer fills the list: a slower answer to an older query is // dropped. While a search is out, the previous results stay in view but can't run: nothing is // highlighted, the list is busy, and the previous announcement is cancelled. findCommands() // stands for the app's search, local or on the server. const status = document.querySelector('.palette-status'); let latest = 0; let pause;  input.addEventListener('input', async () => {   const request = ++latest;   clearTimeout(pause);   highlight(-1);   list.setAttribute('aria-busy', 'true');   let commands = null;   try {     commands = await findCommands(input.value);   } catch {     // shown below, if this is still the latest search   }   if (request !== latest) return;   list.replaceChildren(...(commands ?? []).map((command) => {     const option = Object.assign(document.createElement('li'), { id: `command-${command.id}`, textContent: command.label });     option.setAttribute('role', 'option');     option.dataset.command = command.id;     if (command.disabled) option.setAttribute('aria-disabled', 'true');     return option;   }));   list.removeAttribute('aria-busy');   highlight(commands?.length ? 0 : -1);   pause = setTimeout(() => { // said once typing pauses, not on every key     const n = commands?.length;     status.textContent = !commands ? 'Search failed. Try again.' : n ? `${n} ${n === 1 ? 'command' : 'commands'}` : 'No matching commands';   }, 500); });

Running commands

  • A navigation command goes to its page and closes the palette.
  • An action runs; when it succeeds, the palette closes and the outcome goes to the app's status region or a toast. When it fails, the palette stays open with the error in text.
  • A command that opens a dialog closes the palette first, so no dialog opens on top of it.
  • A destructive command asks first, in a step of the same dialog: the message, then Cancel and a button named for the action ("Delete 3 projects"). Focus goes to Cancel, which is described by the message, and Escape goes back to the results instead of closing the palette.
  • While a command runs, a second Enter does nothing.

Layers

Layers, bottom to top: the page, sticky bars, dropdowns and popovers, toasts, then modals, which make the rest of the page inert. The project's layering scale wins; native <dialog> and the popover attribute use the top layer and need no z-index. The palette is a modal: a native <dialog> in the top layer, above sticky bars, dropdowns, and toasts.

Appearance

These are suggested defaults; the project's design and tokens win.

  • The panel is up to 640 to 720 px wide and about 12% of the window's height from the top; on phones it fills the screen (100dvh), with the search box at the top and only the results scrolling.
  • Rows are 44 px tall, and the input's text is 16 px, so iOS doesn't zoom into it.
  • Text meets 4.5:1 in both themes, shortcut hints and group labels included: text-neutral-500 is only 3.8:1 on a dark panel. Check the project's own colors.
  • Motion is optional: the panel fades in over 150 ms. Under prefers-reduced-motion: reduce, it appears without movement.

Edge cases

  • No commands to show: say so, and offer a way on, such as the settings or the help page.
  • Thousands of commands: search an index, rank once per query, and render only part of the list.
  • Scopes: a palette for the current project or workspace says so in its label, and lists that context's commands first.

Acceptance checklist

  • [ ] Cmd+K on macOS and Ctrl+K elsewhere open it, Cmd or Ctrl+P is left to the browser, and a visible trigger shows the right shortcut
  • [ ] It's a modal dialog: focus goes into the search box, the rest of the page is inert, and a visible Close button is always there
  • [ ] Escape closes it, even with text in the box, and focus returns to the element that had focus before it opened
  • [ ] The search box is a combobox controlling a listbox; focus stays in it, and aria-activedescendant marks the highlighted command
  • [ ] The first result is highlighted whenever the list changes, so Enter runs it, and the arrows wrap through the results in the order on screen
  • [ ] Space types, and keys that belong to an input method are left to it
  • [ ] The highlighted command has at least 3:1 contrast against what's around it, and follows the pointer only when the pointer moves
  • [ ] A disabled command is reachable with the arrows, and Enter doesn't run it
  • [ ] Only the latest search's answer fills the list, and a failed search says so
  • [ ] While a search is out, the previous results can't run, by Enter or by a click, and nothing is highlighted
  • [ ] One status region says the number of results once typing pauses, and "No matching commands"
  • [ ] A destructive command asks first, with focus on Cancel, and Escape goes back to the results
  • [ ] A command that opens a dialog closes the palette first, and the server checks permission when a command runs
  • [ ] On phones it fills the screen, with 44 px rows and 16 px text
  • [ ] Styles come from the project's styling system and tokens

See also

  • Navigation Bar (Responsive) with Mobile Menu: the bar with the palette's visible trigger.
  • Dashboard Layout with Collapsible Sidebar: dense admin apps with many destinations.
  • Select and Combobox: the same combobox keys, with manual selection, for form fields.
  • Modal Dialog: the modal dialog the palette is built on.
